articles.title: The real reason why Donald Trump is so furiously against AI guardrails
articles.summary: Washington’s biggest question this week: Why is President Donald Trump is so furiously against an AI slowdown in the wake of apocalyptic warnings from some t...
articles.body:
Washington's biggest question this week: Why is President Donald Trump so furiously against an AI slowdown in the wake of apocalyptic warnings from some top industry executives?

The clue is in one word — "hoax" — that he's using to ridicule fears that computerized agents could one day seek to destroy humanity.

When Trump reaches for the H-word, two things are usually happening: He's facing a controversy threatening his political or personal priorities, and he's lost control of the politics.

Trump has long dismissed climate change as a "hoax." So it was a tell that he went on social media to specifically draw an analogy between a planet that is warming despite his denials and the calls for AI controls expressed by leaders in the industry.

By changing reality, Trump frees himself from an obligation to act. In energy policy, that means "drill, baby, drill." His administration has slashed regulation , pleasing oil industry donors. His rants against wind farms suggest he hankers for a 20th-century economy running on carbon.

The Jeffrey Epstein saga is a "Democratic hoax," according to Trump . Searing testimonies from the accused sex offender's victims make this a ridiculous charge. But Trump wants to end the storm over his onetime friend that periodically trips up his administration.

The same is true of another supposed "hoax": the investigations into the Capitol riot on January 6, 2021. The outrage was the culmination of another event Trump wants America to forget: his bid to overturn the 2020 election. The hoax routine worked — it got him back to the White House to wield expansive executive power.

The president seems to hope that by simply branding fears of runaway AI as a hoax, he can make them go away.

One of a president's jobs is to counsel a fearful nation, to examine and explain threats, and to advise whether a national effort must be summoned. "The only thing we have to fear is fear itself," Franklin Roosevelt said at the start of a presidency deep in the Great Depression.

Every commander in chief followed suit in the Cold War. And George W. Bush corralled the country after 9/11, almost exactly 25 years ago.

But even as a political matter, Trump might be advised to take the AI freakout seriously. Americans are worried — not necessarily about extinction, but that the new technology will take their jobs. And by rejecting voter concerns about data centers , the president is leaping onto the wrong side of yet another issue as the GOP braces for tough midterm elections .

But the president's blasé attitude to AI may be traced to a host of political, economic and personality traits that have unleashed turmoil across his two presidencies and that will shape his legacy.

Any signal that AI development may slow would almost certainly trigger a reaction on the markets. As his Iran war sticks Americans with high gas prices and record diesel costs , Trump can't afford any Wall Street turbulence that would hurt 401k accounts and check GDP growth.

He's also showing philosophical objections to a slowdown. His presidency has been about unleashing business to make money, not dialing it back.

Former White House AI czar David Sacks argued over the weekend that by expressing concerns about AI's destructive potential, industry titans were trying to pressure politicians and the public into creating their own "preferred" regulatory system.

Trump is taking a similar approach. "When, in the History of Business, did anyone see the Leaders of an Industry call for Regulation that, if strongly implemented, will drive them into oblivion and bankruptcy?" the president wrote Monday.

Trump's governing style isn't a good fit for this deeply complex issue. He said this week that he's an AI user, but whether that goes beyond posting wild memes depicting himself as various superheroes is unclear. And he gets his news from the traveling printer of his aide Natalie Harp .

At the same time, there's a possibility that's often overlooked in the riotous Washington of the second Trump era: What if the president is going against the tide because he's right about a few things?

This would not be the first time that a new technology has triggered warnings of doom that don't play out. And some skeptics doubt alarmist talk from AI chiefs is genuine, suspecting that they are obliquely talking up the potential of their technology ahead of initial public offerings in the coming months.

And Trump has a serious point that even if the US slows AI development, China probably won't, which would give it a superpower advantage.

Plenty of Democrats feel the same way, including President Joe Biden's former national security adviser Jake Sullivan, who wrote in Foreign Affairs earlier this year that Washington "must up its game" in integrating AI across the military, warning that the US would lose leverage if it failed.

But Trump's vision of his own power and place in history also explain his behavior.

He posted on Monday that America would be fine because it had a "STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT." This might placate some supporters — but even if it's true, it's hardly a viable position. AI will be a generational issue long after he's left office, and Trump, as the incumbent president, has a responsibility to set an early course.

Trump critics might wonder whether his views are shaped by personal considerations, including his ownership of stocks exposed to AI, as disclosed in a recent financial filing. The White House insists his accounts are independently managed by third-party institutions. But ethical questions raised by administration officials regulating industries in which their personal wealth is deeply invested has been a constant shadow over the president's second term.

Trump's resistance to unpleasant truths is also at work.

He's never presented his presidency as a vehicle for confronting far-off threats or to tackle complex problems. He's used it to enact revenge against his enemies, to troll his political foes, to boost his own fame and to invade the psyches of billions of people across the globe.

Trump would never issue the kind of dialectical statement that his first predecessor, President Barack Obama , released on Tuesday. The 44th president said he'd been agonizing over AI for a decade and that it was time for top US leaders to convene a national conversation.

"Whether this technology results in amazing breakthroughs in medicine, energy and education or unleashes huge economic disruptions, greater inequality, and potential catastrophe will depend on the choices that we make right now – choices that should be made not just by the companies involved, but by all of us," Obama wrote.

Some Americans might have hoped from similar from Trump. But he's a rebel and a backlash president. His anti-establishment credentials depend on being an outsider, not a unifier.

And Obama's path ultimately points to a US-led international coalition. Trump hates multinational altruism. "America First" is about doubling down on US power, not watering it down.

If Trump refuses to lead, will Congress step in?

There's no time for serious action before the midterms. But if AI explodes as a top campaign theme, it's likely to drive the legislative agenda of whoever controls the House and Senate next year. And if Republicans suffer a wipeout because of Trump's refusal to listen to voters, they may have an incentive to break with the president.

"I am the Hoax Buster, and I'm right now breaking another Hoax — That AI is going to take over, consume, and destroy the World, and that Robots will be marching into our Cities, and getting rid of us all!" Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday.

articles.title: University drops 'doxxing' probe of Republican students amid widespread backlash over viral cake incident
articles.summary: A viral photo of a "Happy Kirkiversary" cake sparked a University of Utah probe into two College Republicans accused of doxxing a fellow student.
articles.body: Two College Republicans at the University of Utah threatened with disciplinary action stemming from a viral social media incident are now breathing a sigh of relief after the school cleared them of wrongdoing. But one student is now demanding that the school work harder to protect conservative speech on campus. "My message to administration would be that conservative voices on campus need to be protected, not only by the students that try to diminish our voice, but also the administration, including the teachers," Rylie Barnes told Fox News Digital. On Sept. 10, 2026, the one-year anniversary of Charlie Kirk's assassination, a woman approached a group of College Republicans at an event on a campus less than an hour's drive from the murder site, and presented them with a snarky dessert. The words "Happy Kirkiversary" were written in red icing on the white cake. Barnes and Riley Beesley, the chairman of the school's College Republicans chapter, took exception to the stunt on their campus, and Barnes posted a photo of the woman holding the cake to her X account. It quickly went viral and led to an anonymous X user identifying the student as Sara Larsen. "We got a lot of backlash from students here on campus, blaming us for doxxing, creating false allegations and lies on social media about it, and reporting to the school all these false allegations as well. So I don't blame the school for kind of jumping the gun on it," Barnes said. "But I think they did jump the gun, which caused this to get so much backlash on the Republican end, just because there wasn't much of an investigation for us. There was just, ‘we need you to come meet with us,' and in our minds, that wasn't okay because we didn't do anything wrong." Thursday night, the University of Utah sent out a notice confirming that the potential disciplinary matter was closed. "The University of Utah’s Office of the Dean of Students has dismissed an ‘accountability’ inquiry into student Rylie Barnes’ social media posts," the message said. "After receiving clarification from Riley Beesley’s representative on Thursday, Sept. 17, the dean’s office also has dismissed an accountability inquiry into Beesley’s social media posts." That "representative" was Beelsey's attorney. The school added that neither student ever faced expulsion, and that normally they would keep disciplinary matters private, but since the students made it public, they publicly responded. Social media was abuzz, with high-profile figures in the Senate and at the Department of Justice (DOJ) keeping an eye on the matter during the week-long saga. Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, called the investigation "indefensible," adding that if the students were expelled, he would "hire both of them—and then help them find schools where they can complete their degrees without fear of political persecution." "Utah … [what the h---] is going on over there," Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights at the DOJ said in an X post. Barnes said the support from social media was crucial to the pair prevailing against the school. "I definitely think that with the amount of social media presence that we were having and the amount of support, it definitely helped the school do more investigation about this, because I'm glad that they realized that there's more than just one side story here, there's two sides," she said. "And when they did more of an investigation, that's exactly why our case got dismissed because of all the support, and they thought that the allegations these students were making were inaccurate." UNIVERSITY OF TENNESSEE CONDEMNS FLYERS APPEARING TO CELEBRATE CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION The school's College Democrats responded by saying Republicans are "waging a campaign of hate" against them. On Tuesday, the university sent emails to Beesley and Barnes requesting closed-door meetings Wednesday morning with its Student Rights and Responsibilities office. "We received information that, if accurate, may go against this priority and the policy on Student Rights and Responsibilities, and I would like to meet and hear your perspective," says a copy of one of the emails, obtained by Fox News Digital. "The report is regarding an incident that happened on or about September 11, 2026 and allegedly involves you attempting to doxx another University of Utah student over a political issue." The email was sent by the office's assistant director, Jose Morales Diaz. "Doxxing" is the act of publicly revealing, usually online, the personal information of another person, typically with the intent of causing harm to that individual. "We will talk about the information our office received, and you will have an opportunity to give your perspective of the incident if you wish. We will also talk about possible next steps, such as resolutions and educational or restorative measures if appropriate," the email said. 30% OF COLLEGE STUDENTS SAY VIOLENCE ACCEPTABLE WAY TO STOP SPEAKERS ON CAMPUSES, SURVEY FINDS The emails also prohibited the students from recording the meetings. But shortly before the meetings were scheduled to take place, the university abruptly canceled them, according to Beesley. Diaz did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. "We found it distasteful, vile, and disgusting. Parents, alumni, students and donors deserve to know about the radical political ideologies festering on college campuses in Utah," Beesley told Fox News Digital of the cake incident. "Given today's political climate, mocking or expressing support such as this should be taken incredibly seriously and the public sphere has a right to know about the lack of morality being observed among young Democrats and those on the left." He strongly condemned doxxing, and said his group had nothing to do with the release of Larsen's information. He also condemned political violence. "We're observing patterns where those on the left find it comical to make threats, have normalized silencing opposing political viewpoints, and avoid accountability or consequences for glorifying murder," he said. "This must end." CARNEGIE MELLON 'DEEPLY CONCERNED' BY PROFESSOR'S 'HOSTILE AND THREATENING POSTS' ABOUT CHARLIE KIRK'S DEATH The university told Fox News Digital it can't comment on student disciplinary action, citing federal law. But Wednesday night, the school released a statement about the ongoing controversy, which has been going viral online for days and has become a national news story. "In recent days, a dispute between political groups on the University of Utah campus has resulted in allegations of harassment, threats, and the inappropriate sharing or amplification of personal information. The University of Utah is reviewing these accusations consistent with established policies, due process and applicable law," the statement said. "As we conduct this review, the university will continue to simultaneously protect freedom of expression and the safety of our students. Calls to harm someone, including electronic harassment and inappropriate sharing of information, are not protected by free speech," it continued. The school also urged the College Democrats and College Republicans groups on campus to convene with leadership in an attempt to better understand one another. It also condemned violence. COLORADO TPUSA CHAPTER ENROLLMENT 'FLAT' AFTER ELDERLY SUPPORTER WAS STRICKEN BY STUDENT WITH TACO BELL CUP Beesley was subject to an alleged violent threat on campus earlier this year, when a person threatened to "Kirk" him. "It was January 12, we were outside tabling and engaging in debates in a format similar to those organized by, let's say, Turning Point USA," Beesley told Fox News Digital at the time. "And soon after [he] declared to us, 'you should die,' followed by, 'I am going to Kirk you,' which you could only think that means I'm either using your imagination going to shoot you or kill you." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Dean Stewart, then 21, was arrested following the incident. Criminal proceedings against him are ongoing, Beesley said. An X account with the name Sara Larsen made a post on Sept. 11, 2026, apologizing for the cake stunt. Fox News Digital could not independently verify whether the account owner is the student embroiled in the controversy. "Upon reflection, it was wrong for me to celebrate, or perpetuate the celebration of, Charlie Kirk’s death. I apologize for doing so sincerely. Nobody should be murdered or persecuted for their speech," reads the tweet — the only post present on an account with 311 followers that was created in February 2017.

articles.title: Talarico hit with ‘blatant corruption’ allegation over hefty salary from consulting firm, campaign pushes back
articles.summary: James Talarico drew a hefty salary from MAYA Consulting while overseeing the Texas Education Agency that awarded the firm millions in contracts.
articles.body:
Senate Democratic nominee James Talarico is facing Republican accusations of "blatant corruption" over consulting work he performed for a progressive firm while serving on the Texas House's Public Education Committee.

Talarico's campaign has denied the allegation, as the Lone Star State's Senate race enters its final stretch with Talarico leading Paxton in recent polling, potentially impacting the GOP's Senate majority.

Talarico worked with MAYA Consulting, now VIDA Collaborative, from 2019 to 2025, receiving paychecks while the firm secured millions in state contracts from the Texas Education Agency, which he helped oversee as a member of the Public Education Committee.

EXCLUSIVE: Senate Democratic nominee James Talarico, who has repeatedly accused his Republican opponent, Ken Paxton, of corruption, is now facing Republican accusations of "blatant corruption" over consulting work he performed for a progressive firm while serving on the Texas House's influential Public Education Committee. Talarico's campaign has denied the allegation as a "lie."

The Lone Star State's Senate race is entering its final stretch, with Talarico leading Paxton in recent polling. A Republican loss could damage the GOP's chances of retaining its Senate majority.

Paxton has projected confidence that, after emerging from a particularly bitter primary race , Texans will respond to his campaign once they hear his message. Talarico, meanwhile, has continued targeting Paxton through major ad buys, including one in which the Democrat calls him "the most corrupt politician in Texas."

Republicans are now responding with allegations of their own, characterizing Talarico's past arrangement with the consulting firm as a "textbook pay-to-play scheme."

They are pointing to paychecks Talarico received from a firm called MAYA Consulting that simultaneously drew in millions in state contracts awarded by the Texas Education Agency (TEA), which he helped provide oversight to as a member of the Public Education Committee .

Talarico announced he was joining MAYA Consulting in a 2019 Facebook post. In the post, he stated that as a consultant he would be "working with districts, nonprofits, and communities to build excellent and equitable educational opportunities for all our students."

According to a Senate campaign financial disclosure filed in 2025, Talarico worked with MAYA Consulting, which has since been rebranded as VIDA Collaborative, from 2019 until 2025.

During those same years, official legislative records show that Talarico served as a voting member of the Texas House's Public Education Committee from 2019 to 2025. Among its responsibilities, the committee oversees the Texas Education Agency, which awards government contracts to firms for services, including then-MAYA Consulting.

TEA registers from 2021 and 2022 show that the agency awarded MAYA two contracts worth $3.578 million and $1.635 million, respectively. The contracts were related to priorities Talarico was pushing in the Texas House at the time, including addressing learning loss due to Covid-19 .

Meanwhile, Talarico's disclosure shows that he earned $83,333.40 from the nonprofit in 2025, in addition to his $13,904.92 part-time salary as a member of the Texas House of Representatives.

Kassi Longoria, CEO of VIDA Collaborative, confirmed with Fox News Digital that Talarico served as an "independent contractor consultant" with the group from 2019 to 2025. She said that Talarico "has no current role with our organization" and clarified that "during his time at VIDA, his consulting work was structured, specifically to remain separate from his role as a Texas state legislator."

She said that Talarico "never worked under, received compensation from, or was involved in securing any state- or federally-funded contracts." She noted that "as a matter of standard practice, VIDA discloses any outside employment or potential conflicts of interest for our staff — including Rep. Talarico's legislative role — in our proposals when we apply for publicly-funded opportunities" and that "similarly, Rep. Talarico's relationship with VIDA was disclosed in his required public financial disclosure filings."

However, Republican National Committee spokesman Zach Kraft accused Talarico of wrongdoing, calling the Democrat's involvement with MAYA an example of "blatant corruption."

"We are looking at a textbook pay-to-play scheme with James Talarico steering millions in taxpayer funds to his DEI consulting agency under the condition he gets commission through a scam no-show job," Kraft told Fox News Digital.

As a member of the Texas House's Public Education Committee, Talarico was not involved in TEA's process for awarding outside contracts and did not vote on the contracts. Fox News Digital is also not aware of any evidence that Talarico received a commission for contracts awarded to MAYA, a claim that both the organization and Talarico's campaign denied.

Kraft alleged that Talarico is "one of the most morally bankrupt individuals to ever run for public office in Texas."

JT Ennis, a spokesperson for Talarico's campaign, pushed back, saying, "This is a lie."

Ennis said that "James' relationship to MAYA was fully disclosed in compliance with Texas House rules" and that "James had no involvement in MAYA Consulting securing any public contracts and his contract with MAYA barred him from representing MAYA before the Texas Legislature or education agencies."

"Ken Paxton is making up lies about James to distract from the fact that he's been impeached by his own party for bribery, reported to the FBI by his own staff, and indicted for investment fraud for scamming his own friends," Ennis alleged, while adding, "Ken Paxton is the most corrupt politician in Texas, and this November, Republicans, Democrats, and independents will come together to reject Ken Paxton's corruption and stand up to this broken, corrupt political system."

In July 2015, Paxton was indicted on charges that he misled and defrauded tech startup investors and failed to disclose that the startup was paying him to promote its stock. Prosecutors agreed in 2024 to drop the charges under a deal requiring Paxton to pay about $271,000 in restitution, perform 100 hours of community service and complete 15 hours of legal ethics courses. Paxton did not enter a plea under the agreement and was never convicted.

Meanwhile, Madison Cercy, a spokeswoman for Paxton's campaign, told Fox News Digital, "It couldn't be clearer: James Talarico sees Texans tax dollars as his own personal slush fund."

Fox News Digital is not aware of any evidence that Talarico has misused tax dollars.

Cercy called Talarico a "taxpayer-funded DEI consultant whose employer receives millions of dollars from Texans while pushing radical ideology in our schools."

articles.title: Acusado de matar jovem grávida por não querer filho negro é condenado | G1
articles.standfirst: Victor de Souza Rocha é apontado como autor da morte de Kariny Sevalho de Lima, em maio de 2022. Corpo da jovem foi encontrado em área de mata em Manaus com o rosto desfigurado, sinais de agressões e perfurações.
articles.summary: Victor de Souza Rocha foi condenado a 26 anos de prisão pelo feminicídio de Kariny Sevalho de Lima, morta em 2022.
articles.body:
Suspeito foi preso por matar a ex-namorada grávida de sete meses em Manaus — Foto: Divulgação

Victor de Souza Rocha, acusado de matar a namorada, Kariny Sevalho de Lima , foi condenado a 26 anos e seis meses de prisão em julgamento realizado em Manaus , na quinta-feira (17). Segundo as investigações, o crime foi cometido porque a vítima, que tinha 19 anos e estava grávida de três meses, era uma mulher negra e Victor teria declarado a pessoas próximas que " não queria ser pai de um filho preto ".

Kariny foi encontrada morta em uma área de mata no dia 26 de maio de 2023. Segundo a polícia, ela estava com o rosto desfigurado, sinais de agressões e torturas, além de perfurações de arma branca por todo o corpo. Victor foi preso quase seis meses depois, em 21 de novembro .

A sessão ocorreu no Fórum Ministro Enoch Reis e foi presidida pela juíza Danielle Monteiro Fernandes Augusto. Preso desde 2023, Victor compareceu ao julgamento, mas respondeu apenas às perguntas da defesa e dos jurados. Ele negou ter matado a jovem.

Durante a votação, os jurados reconheceram quatro qualificadoras para homicídio, que são circunstâncias previstas em lei que tornam o crime mais grave: motivo torpe, meio cruel, recurso que dificultou a defesa da vítima e feminicídio. Também foram reconhecidos os crimes de aborto provocado por terceiros e ocultação de cadáver.

Com a condenação, a juíza manteve a prisão de Victor e determinou que a pena seja executada imediatamente, sem direito de recorrer em liberdade.

As investigações apontam que Kariny foi à residência de Victor, em 25 de maio de 2023, para conversar com ele sobre a gravidez. Victor teria pressionado a vítima a realizar um aborto e já havia afirmado a amigos da vítima que jamais teria um filho com características negras, informou a polícia.

Os autos indicam que Kariny voltou para casa e revelou a gestação aos pais, que manifestaram apoio. A jovem, então, retornou à casa de Victor para informá-lo que levaria a gravidez adiante.

"As investigações apontam que eles tiveram um desentendimento em razão do autor não ter aceitado o posicionamento da vítima, o que o levou a tirar a vida dela”, explicou o delegado Ricardo Cunha na época do crime.

Segundo testemunhas, o casal foi junto à uma área de mata nas proximidades da residência de Victor. Após alguns minutos, ele retornou do local sozinho e nervoso.

Com a demora de Kariny em retornar para casa, familiares dela foram até a casa de Victor, que informou que a namorada já teria ido embora. O corpo dela foi encontrado no dia seguinte.

A prisão de Victor ocorreu na comunidade Monte Sinai, bairro Cidade Nova, Zona Norte de Manaus. O delegado informou que ao ser preso, ele permaneceu em silêncio.

"Ele estava na casa de familiares. Desde a época do crime ele não havia sido mais visto, tentamos efetuar a prisão dele por diversas vezes, mas ele estava foragido", contou o delegado na ocasião.

articles.title: Vera Lúcia (PSTU) propõe estatal de terras raras e reestatização | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidata ao Palácio dos Bandeirantes pelo PSTU cumpriu agenda de campanha em Bauru (SP) nesta quinta-feira (18), com panfletagem na Unesp e reunião com sindicalistas.
articles.summary: Em Bauru, a candidata Vera Lúcia (PSTU) defendeu a reestatização de bancos e a criação de uma empresa de terras raras para impulsionar o desenvolvimento de São Paulo.
articles.body:
Vera Lúcia (PSTU), candidata ao governo de SP — Foto: TV TEM/Reprodução

A candidata ao governo de São Paulo pelo Partido Socialista dos Trabalhadores Unificado ( PSTU ), Vera Lúcia , defendeu a criação de uma empresa de terras raras durante agenda de campanha em Bauru (SP) nesta quinta-feira (18).

Pela manhã, a candidata distribuiu panfletos na Universidade Estadual Paulista (Unesp) e, em seguida, conversou com trabalhadores no Sindicato dos Bancários de Bauru e Região.

Para alavancar o desenvolvimento econômico de São Paulo, a candidata propôs que todo o sistema bancário seja reunido sob controle público e anunciou o plano de criar uma estatal focada na exploração de minérios de alta tecnologia.

"Isso passa, por exemplo, também, com você ter todos os bancos estatizados, unificados, para você ter controle sobre as operações e o investimento na estrutura do país, como, por exemplo, no estado de São Paulo, nós vamos criar uma empresa de terras raras, que nós possamos ter o controle sobre esse minério altamente importante para o desenvolvimento do próprio estado", declarou a candidata.

Na reunião com os sindicalistas, a candidata criticou a rotina imposta pela busca de resultados nos bancos e cobrou melhorias nas rotinas da categoria, apontando que as cobranças excessivas têm provocado problemas de saúde entre os profissionais.

"Primeiro a luta dos trabalhadores bancários nesse momento por melhores condições de trabalho, porque estão adoecidos e essa coisa da competitividade que é colocada nos bancos através das metas que são buscadas", afirmou a candidata.

Vera Lúcia (PSTU), candidata ao governo de SP, cumpre agenda na Unesp de Bauru (SP) — Foto: TV TEM/Reprodução

A candidata também defendeu que o combate às irregularidades na gestão pública exige o fim das privatizações e a entrega do controle das empresas estatais aos próprios trabalhadores e usuários, que participariam do planejamento até a fiscalização dos serviços.

"Estancaria [a corrupção] porque, para além da estatização, é necessário que o conjunto dos trabalhadores desses respectivos setores, mais a população que é usuária de todos esses serviços, tenham o controle sobre essas empresas, tanto no planejamento, quanto na execução e na fiscalização, isso tudo juntamente com o governo. Isso é o que pode acabar com a corrupção, esse é o mecanismo que nós encontramos", disse.

Vera Lúcia tem 58 anos, nasceu em Inajá (PE) e mora em São Paulo. É operária sapateira e formada em Ciências Sociais pela Universidade Federal de Sergipe (UFS).

Trabalhou no movimento de trabalhadores e na criação de centrais sindicais. Pelo PSTU, a candidata disputa o governo de São Paulo pela primeira vez, já tendo concorrido antes aos cargos de presidente da República e de prefeita da capital paulista.

articles.title: Lula rebate Trump sobre facções: 'Terrorismo foi o 8 de Janeiro' | G1
articles.standfirst: Trump classificou PCC e CV como organizações terroristas e disse que o Brasil falhou no combate. Petista disse que presidente dos EUA 'está atrás' de terras raras brasileiras.
articles.summary: Lula critica classificação de Trump para PCC e CV, afirma que terrorismo foi o 8 de Janeiro e alerta para interesse dos EUA em minerais e petróleo brasileiros.
articles.body:
O presidente Lula durante evento no Rio de Janeiro — Foto: Reprodução/YouTube

O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) afirmou nesta sexta-feira (18) que não aceita a classificação, feita pelos Estados Unidos, do PCC e do CV como organizações terroristas.

Em discurso, o candidato do PT à reeleição disse que "terrorismo" foi o 8 de Janeiro e o planejamento de assassinato de autoridades no contexto da trama golpista.

O presidente deu as declarações ao participar de um evento de apresentação de ações integradas de segurança pública no Rio de Janeiro, onde cumpre agenda nesta sexta.

"Nós precisamos ganhar do crime organizado. E eu não aceito a ideia de que as facções bandidas são terroristas, como diz o [Donald] Trump. Quando o Trump fala em terrorismo, ele fala em terrorismo de Estado, ele não fala da luta e da briga pelo poder. Quem fazia isso? O Bolsonaro tentando dar o golpe no 8 de Janeiro. Isso é terrorismo, pensando em matar Lula, Alckmin e até o Alexandre de Moraes. Isso é terrorismo de Estado", afirmou Lula.

Ainda em relação a Donald Trump, Lula afirmou que o norte-americano tem interesse em recursos minerais brasileiros e que o Brasil precisa ampliar investimentos na segurança nacional.

"O petróleo [da Margem Equatorial] parece que é de melhor qualidade. Então, nós temos que tomar conta disso [...], porque o Trump está aí atrás de minerais críticos, petróleo, terras raras. Não! Isso daqui é nosso. Como vamos controlar 18 mil quilômetros de fronteira sem investimento?", questionou.

🔎A inclusão do Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) e do Comando Vermelho (CV) na lista de organizações terroristas pelos Estados Unidos marca uma mudança de abordagem da Casa Branca em relação às facções brasileiras, enquadrando o combate ao narcotráfico sul-americano como prioridade de segurança nacional e política externa.

Em contrapartida, a diplomacia e autoridades brasileiras manifestaram preocupação com o precedente de possíveis intervenções unilaterais estrangeiras, ressaltando que, perante a legislação nacional, as facções continuam sendo enquadradas como organizações criminosas e que a legislação brasileira já prevê penas duras para essas condutas.

Um relatório divulgado pela administração de Donald Trump nesta semana acusa o Brasil de falhar no combate ao PCC e ao Comando Vermelho , classificando ambas as facções como ameaças à segurança internacional e cobrando medidas urgentes para contê-las.

Em resposta aos apontamentos de Washington, o Ministério da Justiça e o governo brasileiro rejeitaram as alegações, destacando a realização frequente de operações de desarticulação patrimonial das quadrilhas e reforçando que já mantêm acordos bilaterais de inteligência e cooperação ativa com agências norte-americanas para combater o tráfico de drogas e armas.

Sobre segurança pública no Rio, o petista afirmou que bandidos e milicianos deixam a população "assustada" nos bairros, escolas e ruas das periferias. Ele declarou que, se for reeleito, vai retomar territórios ocupados pelas organizações criminosas.

E mencionou a PEC da Segurança Pública em tramitação no Congresso, que amplia a participação da União no setor.

Lula disse ainda que vai criar o Ministério da Segurança Pública para reduzir os índices de violência no país.

articles.title: Ronaldo Caiado diz que aumento do Bolsa Família é compra de votos | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato do PSD à Presidência da República chamou o presidente Lula, que tenta a reeleição, de "ladrão do futuro brasileiro" e afirmou que Jair Bolsonaro "não soube governar".
articles.summary: Ronaldo Caiado critica reajuste do Bolsa Família, chama Lula de "ladrão do futuro" e afirma que Jair Bolsonaro não soube governar o país.
articles.body:
Ronaldo Caiado (PSD), candidato à Presidência, em entrevista à "Gazeta do Povo" — Foto: Reprodução

O candidato do PSD à Presidência da República, Ronaldo Caiado , associou o reajuste do Bolsa Família , anunciado nessa quinta-feira (17) pelo governo Lula , a uma tentativa de "comprar voto por R$ 90". O presidente Lula, que tenta a reeleição, aumentou o benefício de R$ 600 para R$ 691 a partir de outubro.

"À véspera de uma eleição, você vê uma atitude populista como essa aí, de querer dizer: 'Agora eu vou aumentar R$ 91 no Bolsa Família.' Isso é brincar com a inteligência do brasileiro, desrespeitar a inteligência do brasileiro e achar que o cidadão, a 16 dias, pode mudar e comprar o voto por mais R$ 90."

Caiado fez as declarações em entrevista em vídeo transmitida pela "Gazeta do Povo", nesta sexta-feira (18).

Em uma série de perguntas de resposta rápida, o candidato classificou Lula(PT) como "ladrão do futuro brasileiro". Sobre o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL), disse: "Conseguiu unir a direita brasileira, mas não soube governar."

Nessa mesma série, Caiado foi questionado sobre os dois ministros do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) que protagonizam a crise na Corte: André Mendonça, indicado por Jair Bolsonaro , e Alexandre de Moraes, indicado por Michel Temer (MDB).

Em relação a Mendonça, que foi relator do caso Master, o candidato disse: "Resistindo, mas está de uma certa maneira isolada. Mas tem os cumprimentos hoje da população brasileira por ter tido a coragem de desnudar."

Sobre Moraes, que está sob suspeita de envolvimento com o ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro, Caiado afirmou: "Já passou o momento de poder saber que seu comportamento não é compatível com o cargo de ministro do Supremo Tribunal Federal."

O candidato disse ser a favor do impeachment de ministros do STF, de "todos que tiverem motivos para serem impeachmados".

Caiado classificou ainda os atos golpistas de 8 de janeiro , que depredaram e ocuparam as sedes dos Três Poderes em Brasília em 2023, como "uma baderna".

O candidato defende a anistia aos condenados pela tentativa de golpe, entre os quais está Jair Bolsonaro.

Em setembro de 2025, o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro foi condenado a 27 anos e 3 meses de prisão , pelos crimes de organização criminosa armada, tentativa de golpe de Estado, tentativa de abolição violenta do Estado Democrático de Direito, dano qualificado contra o patrimônio da União e deterioração de patrimônio tombado.

articles.title: Moradores de Venceslau contam o que fariam com prêmio da Mega-Sena | G1
articles.standfirst: Bolão de nove cotas feito em Lotérica de Presidente Venceslau (SP) acertou sozinho as seis dezenas. Recompensa milionária foi dividida entre os participantes.
articles.summary: O que você faria se ganhasse na Loteria? Em Presidente Venceslau (SP), essa pergunta deixou de ser apenas uma brincadeira para apostadores de um bolão registrado em uma lotérica.
articles.body:
O que você faria se ganhasse na Loteria? Em Presidente Venceslau (SP), essa pergunta deixou de ser apenas uma brincadeira para apostadores de um bolão registrado em uma lotérica da cidade, que acertou as seis dezenas da Mega-Sena .

O prêmio de R$ 101.970.706,05 será dividido entre nove cotistas . A aposta foi feita com sete números e foi a única do país a acertar a sena no concurso 3.059, sorteado na noite desta quarta-feira (17).

Enquanto os verdadeiros ganhadores ainda não tiveram as identidades divulgadas, moradores que costumam apostar nas lotéricas da cidade já começaram a imaginar o que fariam se a sorte tivesse batido à porta deles.

O vendedor ambulante Izemar Cardoso de Andrade descobriu que o prêmio havia saído na cidade somente na manhã desta quinta-feira (18) quando seguia para trabalhar. Ele disse que, se fosse um ganhador, o primeiro investimento seria uma casa nova.

Depois, Izemar afirmou que deixaria parte do dinheiro aplicado e reservaria outra quantia para viajar.

"Tem que viajar, porque a gente precisa distrair a mente. No mundo que nós vivemos, nós só vivemos para trabalhar… Então a gente tem que trabalhar, mas se divertir também”, relatou Izemar.

Apesar de não saber se algum de seus jogos foi premiado, Izemar continuou apostando: "Lógico [que vou continuar apostando]. Eu vim conferir um jogo que joguei ontem. De repente sou até um ganhador. Mas eu vou ficar jogando aqui, porque a sorte está por aqui”, brincou.

Aposta vencedora da Mega-Sena foi registrada em uma lotérica de Presidente Venceslau (SP) — Foto: Emerson Sanchez/TV TEM

A possibilidade de ter ficado milionário também passou perto do aposentado Orestes Rodrigues Filho. Segundo ele, o bolão vencedor chegou a ser oferecido, mas ele decidiu não comprar.

“A moça aqui [da Lotérica] ofereceu para mim, mas eu não comprei. E eu compro direto”, falou Orestes.

E se tivesse aceitado a oferta, Orestes já sabe para onde iria primeiro: “Ia para o Pantanal e ajudaria todos os filhos".

O técnico em eletrônicos Donizete Ferreira Neves também é frequentador da lotérica onde o bolão foi registrado. Ele, porém, também não está entre os ganhadores.

"Se fosse eu, estaria muito contente. Sempre jogo aqui, nessa loteria", disse.

Para ele, o resultado mudou até a relação da cidade com a sorte. E, se a próxima bolada sair para ele, a família também estaria entre as prioridades.

"Oportunidade não falta. Eu vou ajudar alguém que precisa, da família, principalmente [caso fique rico]", afirmou.

Moradores de cidade de Presidente Venceslau (SP) premiada relatam o que fariam com prêmio da Mega-Sena — Foto: Emerson Sanchez/TV TEM

A aposta vencedora do concurso 3.059 foi registrada em uma lotérica de Presidente Venceslau com sete números e em formato de bolão, dividido em nove cotas.

Os números sorteados foram: 01 - 02 - 07 - 18 - 33 - 35.

O prêmio principal foi de aproximadamente R$ 101,9 milhões, o maior valor destinado a uma única aposta no concurso.

Além do prêmio principal, outra aposta registrada na mesma lotérica acertou cinco números e levou R$ 189.985,68. Também era um bolão de nove cotas, feito com sete números.

Em todo o país, 98 apostas acertaram cinco dezenas e receberam R$ 31.664,29 cada. Outras 6.697 apostas fizeram quatro acertos e levaram R$ 763,77 cada.

O próximo concurso da Mega-Sena tem prêmio estimado em R$ 28 milhões.

As apostas podem ser feitas até as 19h, no horário de Brasília, em qualquer lotérica do país ou pelos canais digitais das Loterias Caixa. É necessário ter 18 anos ou mais para participar.

articles.title: Campanha de Lula: Edinho Silva admite desgaste após crise no STF | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente do PT, Edinho Silva afirmou que a crise institucional atingiu a candidatura do presidente, que, segundo ele, vivia uma situação favorável.
articles.summary: Edinho Silva afirma que a crise institucional no STF atingiu a campanha de Lula e defende reformas no Judiciário para responder ao desgaste eleitoral.
articles.body:
Edinho Silva em entrevista ao Estúdio i, na GloboNews, nesta sexta-feira (18). — Foto: Reprodução

O presidente nacional do PT , Edinho Silva, reconheceu nesta sexta-feira (18) que a crise envolvendo o Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) provocou desgaste na campanha à reeleição do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT).

“Claro que vínhamos em uma situação muito favorável eleitoralmente. Veio essa crise institucional. É inegável que ela atingiu a nossa campanha, desgastou a nossa campanha”, afirmou em entrevista ao Estúdio i, da GloboNews.

Segundo Edinho, o conflito acaba atingindo quem está à frente do governo porque, no senso comum, parte da população não distingue claramente os Três Poderes.

“A sociedade traduz todo o sentimento de mudança, o sentimento antissistema, em quem é governo”, declarou.

Em outro momento da entrevista, o dirigente petista afirmou que a crise “assola todo o ambiente político brasileiro” e “penaliza efetivamente o incumbente, aquele que está no poder, aquele que está à frente do governo”.

Apesar de admitir o impacto na campanha, Edinho afirmou que Lula tem respondido à crise de forma coerente com posições que já defendia. Ele citou a reforma do Judiciário e a responsabilização dos envolvidos em eventuais irregularidades.

“É inegável o desgaste, mas estamos respondendo com decisões coerentes com aquilo que nós sempre defendemos. Tem que haver reforma do Judiciário, e os responsáveis têm que ser penalizados”, declarou.

O presidente do PT afirmou ainda que o questionamento da sociedade ao Judiciário é legítimo e mencionou mudanças que podem ser debatidas, como a definição de idade mínima para integrar as cortes superiores, a adoção de mandatos para ministros e o aumento da participação da sociedade civil no Conselho Nacional de Justiça (CNJ) e no Conselho Nacional do Ministério Público (CNMP).

Ele também rejeitou uma relação direta entre o desgaste do Supremo e o fato de seis dos atuais dez ministros terem sido indicados durante governos petistas — quatro por Lula e dois pela ex-presidente Dilma Rousseff .

“Não consigo fazer esse vínculo tão direto entre as indicações dos governos Lula e Dilma e o desgaste que a Suprema Corte enfrenta. Seria, na minha avaliação, forçar demais a mão”, afirmou.

Para Edinho, a resposta eleitoral da campanha deverá passar pela apresentação de Lula como representante de uma agenda de mudanças. Ele citou, além da reforma do Judiciário, a defesa de uma reforma política e eleitoral.

“O sistema hoje, como está organizado, não responde aos anseios da sociedade. Como tem dito o presidente Lula, o sistema apodreceu. Ele precisa ser reformado, precisa ser alterado para que a gente dê conta dos anseios da sociedade”, disse.

articles.title: PGR dá parecer favorável a pedido de Henrique Vorcaro para realizar exames médicos | G1
articles.standfirst: Pai de Daniel Vorcaro, ex-banqueiro do extinto Banco Master, relatou sintomas de possível crise de diverticulite. Na mesma manifestação, a Procuradoria defendeu que outro investigado da operação 'Compliance Zero' permaneça preso.
articles.summary: Pai de Daniel Vorcaro, ex-banqueiro do extinto Banco Master, relatou sintomas de possível crise de diverticulite. Na mesma manifestação, a Procuradoria defendeu que outro investigado da operação 'Compliance Zero' permaneça preso.
articles.body:
A Procuradoria-Geral da República (PGR) deu parecer favorável ao pedido de Henrique Moura Vorcaro, pai de Daniel Vorcaro, ex-banqueiro do extinto Banco Master, para realizar exames médicos fora da unidade prisional onde está detido.

Em manifestação enviada nesta sexta-feira (18) ao ministro André Mendonça , do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ), o órgão defendeu a autorização para os procedimentos solicitados pela defesa.

Segundo os advogados, Henrique Vorcaro apresentou sintomas de uma possível crise de diverticulite e procurou uma unidade de pronto atendimento próxima ao presídio.

O pedido de autorização para os exames ocorre dois dias após a defesa solicitar ao STF a revogação da prisão preventiva de Henrique Vorcaro ( leia mais abaixo ).

A defesa afirmou, na manifestação desta sexta, que ele pediu autorização para ser atendido pelo coloproctologista Fábio Lopes Queiroz e para realizar exames complementares indicados pelo médico.

No parecer assinado pelo procurador-geral da República, Paulo Gonet Branco, a PGR concluiu pelo deferimento do pedido. A decisão final cabe ao ministro relator.

Henrique Vorcaro foi preso em maio deste ano sob suspeita de integrar o chamado “núcleo violento” do grupo criminoso associado ao ex-banqueiro preso, segundo uma fonte da Polícia Federal.

A prisão aconteceu em Nova Lima, na Região Metropolitana de Belo Horizonte.

PGR é contra soltura de outro investigado

Na mesma manifestação, a Procuradoria se posicionou contra o pedido de revogação da prisão preventiva de Rodrigo Pimenta Franco Avelar Campos, investigado na operação "Compliance Zero".

Segundo a PF, o grupo atuava em ataques cibernéticos, invasões telemáticas e monitoramento ilegal e teria sido usado para atender interesses da organização investigada.

Na decisão que autorizou a operação, ele aparece como colaborador de David Henrique Alves, líder operacional do grupo, e teria executado tarefas como pagamento de boletos e aquisição de domínios de internet.

Ao pedir a soltura, a defesa argumentou que Rodrigo está preso há mais de 90 dias sem oferecimento de denúncia e afirmou que ele não exercia função de comando dentro da organização investigada.

Os advogados também sustentaram que não há risco de retomada das supostas atividades criminosas e sugeriram a substituição da prisão por medidas cautelares.

A PGR, porém, afirmou que permanecem presentes elementos de materialidade e autoria que justificaram a prisão preventiva.

Segundo o órgão, ainda há diligências em andamento e os fundamentos que embasaram a medida continuam válidos.

No parecer, a Procuradoria também citou risco de reiteração criminosa e de fuga.

Ao reproduzir trechos da decisão que decretou a prisão, o documento afirma que Rodrigo teria atuado como colaborador técnico e logístico do núcleo "Os Meninos", participando de atividades ligadas à estrutura digital do grupo.

articles.title: STJ mantém condenação de ex-deputada Flordelis a 50 anos de prisão | G1
articles.standfirst: Sexta Turma também confirmou decisão do Tribunal de Justiça do Rio que anulou a absolvição da neta biológica da ex-deputada, e de dois filhos adotivos.
articles.summary: Sexta Turma também confirmou decisão do Tribunal de Justiça do Rio que anulou a absolvição da neta biológica da ex-deputada, e de dois filhos adotivos.
articles.body:
Por unanimidade, a Sexta Turma do Superior Tribunal de Justiça (STJ) manteve a condenação da ex-deputada Flordelis a 50 anos de prisão, pela morte do pastor Anderson do Carmo, então seu marido, em 2019. A decisão foi tomada na quarta-feira (16).

O STJ confirmou o entendimento do tribunal do júri que, em 2022, sentenciou Flordelis pelos crimes de homicídio triplamente qualificado consumado, homicídio duplamente qualificado tentado, associação criminosa armada e uso de documento falso.

Flordelis foi condenada por arquitetar o crime, que ocorreu na casa da família, em Niterói (RJ). Anderson do Carmo foi morto a tiros. O crime teria sido motivado pelo controle das finanças da família e pela forma rígida como o pastor administrava os conflitos entre os integrantes.

A Sexta Turma do STJ também manteve a decisão do Tribunal de Justiça do Rio de Janeiro (TJRJ) que anulou a absolvição da neta biológica da ex-deputada, Rayane dos Santos Oliveira, e de dois filhos adotivos, Marzy Teixeira da Silva e André Luiz de Oliveira.

A defesa da ex-deputada alegou ao STJ que a condenação era nula por irregularidades no processo, como falta de fundamentação das qualificadoras do crime.

Relatora do caso, a desembargadora convocada Nilsoni de Freitas afirmou que o entendimento consolidado do STJ é no sentido de que, no processo penal, um ato só pode ser declarado nulo se houver a demonstração de prejuízo concreto, o que não ocorreu no caso.

Flordelis durante o primeiro dia de júri — Foto: Brunno Dantas/TJRJ

A relatora afirmou que as circunstâncias do crime foram especificadas, como – motivo torpe, meio cruel e recurso que impossibilitou a defesa da vítima.

Ressaltou ainda que isso foi baseado em provas periciais e testemunhais, o que demonstra a existência de fundamentação suficiente para a decisão de submissão do julgamento ao júri.

“Não há decisão silente, mas pronúncia concisa, como tolerado nessa fase”, afirmou a desembargadora.

articles.title: Reajuste do Bolsa Família: AGU pede que STF valide novo valor | G1
articles.standfirst: O piso do programa passou de R$ 600 para R$ 691. O reajuste passa a valer em outubro, com pagamentos a partir do dia 19, entre o primeiro e o segundo turno das eleições.
articles.summary: O reajuste do Bolsa Família eleva o piso para R$ 691 em outubro, e a AGU argumenta ao STF que a medida apenas cumpre a atualização periódica do benefício.
articles.body:
A Advocacia-Geral da União (AGU) pediu nesta sexta-feira (18) que o Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) reconheça que o decreto que reajustou em 15,04% os valores do Bolsa Família é constitucional.

O piso, mantido em R$ 600 desde o início do terceiro mandato de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), sobe para R$ 691. O reajuste passa a valer em outubro, com pagamentos a partir do dia 19, entre o primeiro e o segundo turno das eleições.

Segundo o Ministério do Planejamento, o aumento no Bolsa Família vai custar, em 2026, R$ 5,8 bilhões e, em 2027, o impacto do reajuste nas contas públicas será de quase R$ 23 bilhões.

O pedido do governo ao Supremo foi feito em uma ação na qual o tribunal determinou que a partir de 2022 fosse implementado o pagamento do programa de renda básica de cidadania para os brasileiros em situação de extrema pobreza e pobreza.

Em junho de 2024, o relator, Gilmar Mendes, reconheceu que o Programa Bolsa Família é uma etapa da implementação progressiva da renda básica de cidadania, submetendoseus valores ao regime de atualização periódica.

Um dia antes da edição do decreto do Bolsa Família, a Defensoria acionou o Supremo pedindo que o Executivo se manifestasse sobre a pendência de atualização dos valores.

"Registre-se que o decreto não institui benefício novo, não cria categoria adicional de beneficiários, não altera o critério legal de elegibilidade e não inaugura programa social. Trata-se, ao contrário, de providência voltada à preservação, no tempo, do cumprimento da ordem injuncional, ao implementar a atualização periódica dos valores expressamente prevista no marco legal já reconhecido por essa Suprema Corte como apto a concretizar a decisão proferida nestes autos. Limita-se, assim, a preservar o valor real de prestações integrantes de política pública permanente, mediante aplicação da variação acumulada do INPC, sem modificação da arquitetura normativa do Programa Bolsa Família", disse a AGU.

O governo pede que o Supremo reconheça que o decreto foi editado em conformidade com o quadro constitucional e legal.

"[O reajuste] constitui providência idônea à preservação, no tempo, do cumprimento da ordem injuncional, inserindo-se no processo gradual de implementação das medidas destinadas à concretização dos comandos constitucionais de erradicação da pobreza e da marginalização e de redução das desigualdades sociais e regionais, do qual decorreu, entre outras providências, a edição da Lei nº 14.601/2023, que 'prevê que os valores “poderão ser corrigidos a cada intervalo de, no máximo, 24 (vinte e quatro) meses, na forma estabelecida em regulamento, vedada sua redução'", diz a AGU.

articles.title: Pessoas com deficiência no Brasil: IBGE revela desigualdades | G1
articles.standfirst: O IBGE divulgou a 2ª edição do informativo Pessoas com Deficiência e as Desigualdades Sociais no Brasil, com dados do Censo Demográfico 2022. Veja cinco destaques.
articles.summary: Dados do Censo 2022 mostram que pessoas com deficiência no Brasil enfrentam maior analfabetismo e menor ocupação, apesar do avanço no serviço público federal.
articles.body:
Fachada IBGE AMAPÁ — Foto: Crystofher Andrade/g1

Nesta sexta-feira (18) o Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística ( IBGE ) divulgou a 2ª edição do informativo Pessoas com Deficiência e as Desigualdades Sociais no Brasil, com dados do Censo Demográfico 2022.

Em 2022, havia 14,4 milhões de pessoas com deficiência (PCDs) no Brasil. Isso representa cerca de 7,3% da população, sendo 6,03% com deficiência severa (muita dificuldade em alguma função) e 1,23% com deficiência profunda.

🔎A publicação utiliza, além dos dados do último Censo, fontes complementares como Pesquisa de Informações Básicas Municipais (MUNIC); o Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE); Censo Escolar e Censo da Educação Superior, do INEP; e dados do Ministério da Gestão e da Inovação em Serviços Públicos.

Confira destaques da divulgação em cinco gráficos:

Entre as pessoas com deficiência, a dificuldade mais comum é para enxergar, que atinge 4,0% da população. Em seguida vêm as dificuldades para caminhar ou subir degraus (2,6%) e para pegar objetos pequenos (2,0%). Dificuldades associadas a funções mentais e a mais de uma limitação simultânea aparecem empatadas, com 1,4% cada, e a dificuldade para ouvir atinge 1,3% da população.

IBGE: Dificuldades de PCDs — Foto: Arte/g1

A renda do trabalho tem peso menor na composição da renda de domicílios com moradores com deficiência. Nesses lares, o trabalho responde por 55,7% da renda total, enquanto outras fontes como aposentadorias, pensões e benefícios sociais somam 44,3%.

Já nos domicílios sem pessoas com deficiência, o trabalho é a fonte predominante, com 78,4% da renda, contra apenas 21,6% de outras fontes.

IBGE: trabalho tem menor participação na renda de domicílios com PCDs — Foto: Arte/g1

articles.title: Trump refers to Black man from racially offensive 1988 campaign ad while stumping in North Carolina
articles.summary: As President Donald Trump tries to convince voters that Democrats have let crime run amok, he's digging into the country's political past to cite one of the...
articles.body:
As President Donald Trump tries to convince voters that Democrats have let crime run amok, he's digging into the country's political past to cite one of the most controversial campaign advertisements that relied heavily on racist tropes.

During a campaign stop Wednesday in Gastonia, North Carolina, to stump for Republican U.S. Senate candidate Michael Whatley, Trump resurrected a 1988 George H.W. Bush presidential campaign ad featuring Willie Horton, a Black man convicted of rape and assault after his release through a Massachusetts prison furlough program.

A grainy black-and-white prison photo of Horton was used in the ad targeting then-Massachusetts Gov. Michael Dukakis, who was ahead of Bush in the polls. On Wednesday, Trump evoked the Horton ad in an effort to convince voters Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper, Whatley's opponent in the Senate race, is soft on crime.

"Willie Horton was a bad guy, really bad guy," Trump said, before comparing Dukakis's release of Horton to the pretrial release of a Black man who faces a murder charge for last year's killing of a white Ukrainian refugee in Charlotte, North Carolina.

But Cooper was not the governor when the man was released or when he was later charged with killing the refugee.

"Same thing as this, same as, same exact thing," the president told the crowd in Gastonia.

It's the second time Trump has invoked Willie Horton while campaigning for his party. Last month during a speech in Las Vegas, Trump called the Charlotte killing a "Willie Horton — modern day" tragedy.

"After the Willie Horton ad dropped, Bush established a lead in the polls and never looked back," said Andra Gillespie, a political scientist at Emory University outside Atlanta. "They showed the picture, and you ascribed race onto it. It wasn't sufficiently condemned as racism."

A spokeswoman for the Republican National Committee, which organized the Gastonia campaign rally, defended Trump's reference to Horton.

"Roy Cooper emptied prisons and released thousands of violent monsters onto North Carolina streets," RNC National Press Secretary Natalie Baldassarre said in a statement to The Associated Press. "The results had deadly consequences, and every Democrat who supports abolishing or defunding the police, paroling criminals, and implementing lax bail policies will have to answer for their dangerous records in November."

Trump paints North Carolina as a 'dangerous state'

Wednesday's rally cited the Aug. 22, 2025, killing of white 23-year-old Iryna Zarutska on a commuter train in Charlotte.

Decarlos Brown Jr., who is Black, faces murder and other charges in Zarutska's stabbing, which was captured on video. Court records showed that at the time of the attack, Brown had 14 prior cases in Mecklenburg County, including serving five years for robbery with a dangerous weapon. Doctors had diagnosed him with schizophrenia.

Republicans and other influential voices in Trump's Make America Great Again movement claimed the attack showed how Democratic elected leaders in large cities across the U.S. failed to protect residents, while some conservative commentators suggested Democrats were ignoring an unfounded "black-on-white" crime problem .

"He should have been locked up for many, many years," Trump said Wednesday of Brown.

"Nobody used to think of North Carolina as a dangerous state, criminally dangerous," Trump added while blaming Cooper. "It was apple pie, right? Now, it's one of the most violent, one of the worst in the whole nation."

According to 2024 FBI crime data, North Carolina ranked 19th for statewide violent-crime rates in a 50-state comparison.

During the Gastonia rally, a mosaic of mug shots was displayed on a large screen for the crowd. Trump claimed Cooper had cut a deal with "radical activists" to release "some of the worst criminals in the nation into North Carolina."

"He released these people. This is just a small group of them," the president said, pointing to the mug shots that overwhelmingly featured Black people.

Although it is unclear under what circumstances the people in the mug shots were released, state corrections officials have said Brown was not released early from prison or under Cooper's COVID-era prisoner-release settlement that Trump referenced.

Before fatally stabbing Zarutska, according to court records, Brown had been on a pretrial release over a misdemeanor offense that was ordered by a magistrate after Cooper left office.

Republicans are under pressure to win over swayable voters as the November midterms approach with Democrats pushing to gain control of the House, the Senate, or both. Some political strategists say part of the ploy of adding Horton to the North Carolina Senate campaign is to rile up Trump's base.

"He's tapping into the anger to remind Republican voters of what he thinks their first principles are in hopes that will be successful for Republican candidates," Gillespie said.

"He's doing this to try and divert attention away from criticism of how he's governing at the moment," she added. "Democrats want to make the story of this election Trump's low approval numbers, the war in Iran, inflation, being preoccupied with things that don't make a whole lot of sense when there are really serious things going on in the country."

Dewey Clayton, professor emeritus of political science at the University of Louisville, said Trump and other Republicans may be thinking that what worked before in the 2016 and 2024 elections presumably will work again in this year's midterms.

"It was very effective," Clayton said. "You do not necessarily have to look at it as racial, in and of itself, although (race) clearly becomes a component. In 2026, talking about ads going back in the 1980s? I'm sure he had consultants that were basically saying this is tried and true."

The GOP may need the push in November, Gillespie warns. "I think the motivation by going back to these old strategies is there is real concern about Republican enthusiasm and you might see lower Republican turnout," she said.

Rhetoric attempts to divert voters' attention from rising costs

The tactic speaks to desperation by Trump and the Whatley campaign, according to Morgan Jackson, a partner with Nexus Strategies in Raleigh.

"Trump brings up Willie Horton to stoke racial division, something he's used for the last 10 years," said Jackson, who is chief strategist for Cooper's campaign . "It is very clear from the president's speech last night their only goal is to sow division and hate and lies. Michael Whatley doubles down in support of that effort."

Jackson also said Trump and Whatley are trying to change the election's message of "rising inflation and the cost of everything."

"They want to use inflammatory rhetoric, hate speech and lies to sow division in a chance to win an election," he said. "By referencing Willie Horton, they are showing their hand very clearly."

The AP sent an email Thursday seeking comment from Whatley's Senate campaign.

Williams reported from Detroit. AP videojournalist Erik Verduzco in Gastonia, North Carolina, contributed.

articles.title: Why Democrats are starting to feel bullish about a midterm wave
articles.summary: Democrats' wary optimism about the midterms gave way to growing confidence this week. The party has seen strong post-Labor Day polls in key battlegrounds - a...
articles.body:
Democrats' wary optimism about the midterms gave way to growing confidence this week.

The party has seen strong post-Labor Day polls in key battlegrounds - and even in traditionally red areas. Recent escalations in the war in Iran, including an attack on a major pipeline in Saudi Arabia, mean the rising gas prices bedeviling Republicans will not be going down anytime soon. Republicans have not been able to bring prices under control more generally. And President Donald Trump's unpopularity is at near-record levels.

Considering all this, Democrats now think conditions are right for the party to retake control of the House and possibly the Senate later this year.

"If the election were held today, we would win the majority," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (New York) said in an interview with The Washington Post.

Schumer said he felt "considerably more bullish" about Democrats' chances of retaking the Senate than he did a few months ago. He described the environment as uncannily similar to 2006, when discontent with the war in Iraq helped Democrats recapture the Senate and the House.

House Minority Whip Katherine Clark (D-Massachusetts) said Democrats' recent momentum is driven by their focus on the economy, with voters believing that the party understands the financial pain they've felt in the years since Republicans swept into unified control.

"That is what is driving these polls," Clark told The Post on Thursday.

Democrats need at least four more seats to take the Senate majority and would have to win at least two in states Trump carried by double-digit margins in 2024. Republicans are seeking to blunt any Democratic gains by flipping Democratic-held open seats in Michigan and New Hampshire, where polls show competitive races. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report shifted its rating of the Senate contest in New Hampshire from "Lean Democrat" to "Toss Up" this week.

Republicans focused on keeping control of the House argue that they have a more favorable map, partly because a GOP redistricting effort has limited the number of battleground districts, and partly because they believe that Democratic primary voters nominated weak candidates in a handful of key races.

Then there is the incoming flood of GOP money.

Republicans are set to spend nearly $140 million more on ads than Democrats are in the nine most competitive races in the final weeks of the campaign, according to ad tracking firm AdImpact. The disparity is especially yawning in the Senate contest in Texas, where Republicans have reserved $39.6 million in ads and Democrats have reserved just $5.1 million.

On the House side, the National Republican Congressional Committee plans to run coordinated ads in 39 districts, with more than $24 million in ads reserved.

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has plans for coordinated ads in 14 districts.

"The Republican campaign engines are firing on all cylinders, and we are burying House Democrats in battleground districts across the country," said Mike Marinella, spokesperson for House Republicans' campaign arm. "Republicans have the historic fundraising advantage, a more favorable map, stronger candidates, and the firepower to defy history and grow our House majority."

Schumer acknowledged Republicans' financial advantage but said it would not stop Democrats from retaking the Senate.

"We don't need as much money as them given the political climate, given the terrain," he said. "All we need is enough to stay in the ballpark and be able to answer them."

Republicans have begun to openly acknowledge electoral concerns in recent weeks, particularly with polls showing that Democrats are far more eager to vote than Republicans are.

Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana) told reporters Thursday that he was going to Kansas, Nebraska and Iowa to raise money for GOP Senate candidates.

"If you told me six months ago I was going to be having to spend my time in those three states, I wouldn't have believed you. Those ought to be fat guy layups for us," he said, though he predicted Republicans would hold those seats.

"The far left, they're angry," Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) said this week on the "Pod Force One" podcast, describing this as a "challenging environment" for his party. "They hate President Trump with a burning passion. And they're going to crawl over broken glass to vote."

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-South Dakota) acknowledged Wednesday that Republicans are facing "headwinds" but said the Senate races that will decide control of the chamber remain competitive.

"It's not a great environment for us," Thune said. "But we've got really quality candidates in all the competitive races, and the polling that we're seeing in those races shows that these races are tight."

Republicans have been debating how to increase enthusiasm beyond spending more money. Some, largely those closely tied to the president and his political operation, argue that the path to victory is to re-create the electorate Trump built in 2024. Other Republicans - primarily those in battleground districts where private and public polls show that voters are deeply upset with the president - believe the way to win is to distance themselves from the administration and its policies, a difficult task following a decade of Trump remaking the party in his own image.

"I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot," Trump said during one of two speeches he gave at the Republicans' midterm convention in Dallas recently. "Just one more time."

Trump has made it difficult for many candidates, especially those in tight races, to embrace this tactic. In large part, that's because he has repeatedly dismissed the issue that voters say is their main stressor: prices. His trade war has raised prices on goods across the country. And gas prices, which have shot up because of the president's war against Iran, are nearing $4.50 per gallon on average.

However, speaking at a campaign rally Wednesday in North Carolina, a state he has won in three straight presidential elections, Trump said high fuel prices were "a very inexpensive price to pay for what we have done" in Iran.

A Republican operative working on House races, speaking on the condition of anonymity to be candid, responded to Trump's comments with an animated image of actor Bryan Cranston screaming, "F---!"

The president has promised to get out the vote for Republican candidates, including those in trouble deep in Trump country. Some have taken him up on his offer, but not every candidate wants him around, and administration officials' visits to red states have been seen as warning signs for Republicans.

Vice President JD Vance traveled to Kansas this week to stump for Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, who is in a tighter-than-expected race against Democrat Adam Hamilton. Trump and Vance won Kansas by 16 percentage points in 2024.

Vance is also set to campaign in Iowa on Friday. But the state's Republican Senate nominee, Rep. Ashley Hinson, will not appear next to the vice president. A Hinson spokesperson cited previously scheduled events, but the absence comes as the candidate seeks to tout her bipartisan record in a state Trump won by 13 percentage points in 2024. Hinson is locked in a tight race against Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek.

And in South Florida, an area Trump dominated in 2024, Republican Rep. María Elvira Salazar openly broke with the president Thursday.

"Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far," Salazar says directly to the camera in a new campaign ad. "The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today."

Democrats say they began to see a change during what was supposed to be Republicans' hallmark 2026 event: the party's unorthodox midterm convention. The gathering was billed as a way for the GOP to showcase its front-line candidates, but instead it featured Trump defending his record and pledging to give each American adult a $5,000 check if Republicans hold Congress this year, a proposal many Democrats saw as a sign of desperation.

"We're not measuring the drapes, but the ground has shifted," said Xochitl Hinojosa, a longtime Democratic operative and top spokesperson at the Democratic National Committee after the 2016 election.

Some Democratic operatives running campaigns said they had been waiting to see whether Republicans would coalesce around a clear affordability message during the Texas event. But when it became obvious that the event would be a Trump-centric celebration that offered no direct case for why Republicans deserved unified control for two more years, their confidence grew.

"Turns out breaking all your campaign promises and doing everything possible to make life more expensive for everyone is bad politics," said Viet Shelton, spokesperson for House Democrats' campaign arm. "Shocker."

The last time Democrats experienced a wave election was in 2018, when the party swept into control of the House two years after Trump's first presidential win.

Meredith Kelly, a Democratic operative who was the top spokesperson at House Democrats' campaign arm at the time, said that there are plenty of similarities between that year and this one - primarily around Trump's unpopularity - but that the biggest difference is how Republicans' worries are coming from voters who helped them win in 2024, such as rural voters and Black and Latino men.

"Their coalition's floor is falling out from underneath them," said Kelly.

The prospect of a wave election has Democratic candidates in districts once thought entirely unreachable for the party feeling like they may have a shot to do the unexpected in November.

Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy veteran running against GOP Rep. Lauren Boebert in a district that spans eastern Colorado, knows that her odds of winning have always been long. Trump won the district less than two years ago by 18 percentage points. But powered almost entirely by anger at Washington and voters' fears about their personal finances, Laubacher thinks she has an opportunity to take down her outspoken Republican opponent.

"People vote frequently about their pocketbooks and their wallets, but I think the situation is growing ever more fraught for people," said Laubacher. "Every aspect of their life has become more expensive, and they do not feel that the government is doing anything about any of it."

Jarrell Dillard contributed to this report.

articles.title: Ex-Dem insider reveals why Biden's daughter threatened to sue her: 'Bordered on parody'
articles.summary: Lindy Li reveals Ashley Biden threatened to sue her over claims about Joe Biden's cognitive decline, sharing screenshots of the since-deleted post.
articles.body: Ashley Biden, the daughter of former President Joe Biden and First Lady Jill Biden, threatened to sue a former Democratic fundraiser for spilling secret internal discussions about her father’s cognitive and political decline in the 2024 presidential election. Lindy Li, a former Democratic fundraiser who switched her party affiliation over unheeded warning signs about Biden's decline in the 2024 election, said Ashley Biden posted the threat to Instagram in February of last year. "They wanted to scare me. That was the goal," Li told Fox News Digital. Li’s account of the threat, in her view, was one of the many attempts to intimidate her that she received after deciding to speak out about the fear, disorganization and secrecy that had paved the path for Biden to run for re-election in 2024 despite looming concerns about his age. Also, the fact that those threats never materialized is evidence to Li that even her critics recognize the validity of her testimony. EX-DEM FUNDRAISER TORCHES BIDEN AS BOOK LAUNCH IMPLODES: 'NO ONE WANTS TO READ' Li described the threat from Ashley Biden in her book, "Unburdened." "Ashley later threatened to sue me for saying there was a cover-up of her father’s decline, lashing out on Instagram with a bravado so crude it bordered on parody: ‘This woman is a bonavide [sic] liar. Karma is a real bad b----, Lindy,’" she wrote. "’I don’t know you but can’t wait to meet your a-- in court. Ready for a lawsuit? Let’s go! I won’t put up with this BS anymore.’" In an interview with Fox News Digital, Li showed screenshots of the post, which she said was taken down just a day later. She recalled thinking it was odd; beyond the lawsuit threat, Ashley Biden claimed she didn’t know who Li was. But Li had met Ashley Biden on a number of occasions and shared pictures of the two of them with Fox News Digital as proof. "Doesn’t even pass the smell test," Li said. EX-DEM INSIDER DROPS BOMBSHELL ON WHERE HARRIS RANKED IN SECRET POLL FOR BIDEN REPLACEMENTS As a top fundraiser for both Biden and Harris, Li worked closely with top donors, high-profile members of the party and the Democratic National Committee (DNC). When she decided to go public with revelations about Biden’s age, she said the retaliation began immediately. "When I went on Shannon’s show to say Biden needs to step aside — and three hours later he did — my access immediately vanished and all my fears about speaking up were justified," Li told Fox News Digital. "I knew that if I spoke up my life would be ruined and frankly, in that respect, it was. I was never invited to the White House again, never spoke to Biden again. Prior to that, I was invited to the White House every two to three weeks. There was always some event." When Li brought Ashley Biden’s threat to her legal representation, her lawyers dismissed the possibility but said that the Bidens would likely try to avoid a painful disclosure battle that could drag more details into the public eye over his cognitive decline. EX-DEM INSIDER EXPOSES WHAT HARRIS TOLD TOP DONORS DAYS BEFORE BIDEN DROPPED OUT: 'INSULTING' "My lawyer’s eyes lit up: ‘You want her to use you. The discovery would be incredible,’" she recalled. "Truth, after all, remains the strongest shield against defamation." "Everything I said was true so... I’m still waiting to hear exactly what I said that is legally actionable," Li said.
