articles.title: Why Trump’s new rule for green card applicants is sparking controversy
articles.summary: A new Trump administration rule that is expected to make it harder for many legal immigrants to obtain green cards if they receive or are deemed likely to ne...
articles.body:
A new Trump administration rule that is expected to make it harder for many legal immigrants to obtain green cards if they receive or are deemed likely to need public assistance went into effect Friday – even as lawsuits seeking to halt it wind their way through federal court.

The effort is one of President Donald Trump's latest moves to curb the number of immigrants in the US, including residents already living here legally.

What's more, the rule could prompt many green card applicants and their families to forgo receiving needed federal aid to avoid becoming considered "public charges" and hurting their chances of being approved.

Here's what you need to know about Trump's changes to the "public charge" rule:

Federal immigration officers have long reviewed green card applicants to ascertain whether they have the financial means to support themselves, among other considerations, to obtain permanent residency.

The Immigration Act of 1882 allowed the US government to deny entry to applicants deemed likely to be unable to take care of themselves and wind up dependent on government assistance – in other words, become "public charges."

In 1999, the Clinton administration defined a public charge as someone "primarily dependent" on government benefits. It considered only cash aid, such as Temporary Assistance for Needy Families or Supplemental Security Income, and Medicaid for long-term institutional care.

The first Trump administration sought to widen that definition to encompass non-cash benefits, such as food stamps, Medicaid and housing subsidies. It announced the broader rule in 2019 and put it into effect in 2020.

However, the following March, a federal court nullified the rule, and the Biden administration rescinded it. Biden officials then issued a new rule in 2022 limiting consideration to cash benefits only and clarifying that family members' use of federal benefit programs does not have an impact on applicants' reviews.

What does the new Trump administration rule do?

The new rule is similar to what was implemented by the first Trump administration but more expansive.

The latest rule, published in July, allows immigration officers to consider a wider array of public assistance programs when determining whether green card applicants will likely become "public charges." It also rescinds the 2022 rule.

"Under @POTUS Trump, DHS is restoring the basic principle that immigrants must be able to support themselves," the Department of Homeland Security posted to X at the time. "We are reaffirming the requirement of self-reliance, protecting public resources, and ending policies that encouraged dependency on hard-working American taxpayers."

The new rule does not specify which safety net programs should be considered, saying only that DHS "will consider the receipt of any means tested public benefits."

That could potentially include a wider array of income-based assistance, such as food stamps, Medicaid, childcare subsidies, housing vouchers and Head Start, as well as certain tax breaks, such as the child tax credit, Maddie Geschu, director of policy and advocacy at the Protecting Immigrant Families Coalition, told CNN in July.

Also, the new rule allows immigration officers to consider government benefits applied for on behalf of family members, including children who are citizens.

About 588,000 applicants are subject to public charge reviews annually, on average, according to DHS.

But the so-called "chilling effect" could have an even wider impact as applicants and their families opt to stay away from safety net programs for fear of being denied green cards.

DHS estimates that about 950,000 people may opt to leave or not enroll in six public benefits programs it examined, including Medicaid, food stamps, the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) and federal rental assistance.

Undocumented immigrants would not be affected since they do not qualify for public aid.

Immigration advocates fear that the rule will deter eligible family members from applying for or remaining enrolled in public safety net programs, including school meals and WIC, which provides nutrition assistance and counseling to pregnant women, new mothers and young children.

"No parent should ever have to choose between feeding their children and keeping their family together," Clarissa Hayes, deputy director of child nutrition programs and policy at the Food Research & Action Center, told reporters earlier this week. "We cannot allow fear and confusion to determine whether or not a child will have enough to eat."

Also, the revised rule "really opens the green card process to abuse based on partisan politics or personal bias," Geschu told reporters.

Earlier research on the prior Trump administration rule found that participation in programs among immigrant families and citizen children declined in 2019 and 2020, even among those not subject to it at the time, the advocates said.

Similarly, the latest effort would have widespread consequences. Some 3.7 million members of immigrant households could lose Medicaid, food stamps, housing benefits and other assistance, according to a George Washington University study published in December that analyzed the proposed rule. State economies could lose $27.4 billion as healthcare providers, grocery stores and other businesses lose revenue. Up to 212,000 jobs could be lost.

Why have some states and cities filed lawsuits?

A coalition of 22 states and the District of Columbia, led by New York, are suing to block the rule. A group of cities, led by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, has filed a similar lawsuit. They were both filed Monday in the Southern District of New York.

The states argue they would lose billions of dollars in federal funding if immigrants, particularly mixed-status families, disenroll from safety net programs due to fears about immigration consequences. And they say that the new rule gives "unfettered discretion for immigration officials to determine who can be excluded on public charge grounds."

The determinations could "fundamentally depart from the core meaning of the term" public charge, according to the filing.

The cities, meanwhile, say in their filing that the rule will harm their public health and economic interests, including shifting costs for healthcare, food and housing to the cities and hurting their labor forces.

A group of advocacy organizations filed their own lawsuit against the rule in the Southern District of New York on Thursday, arguing it violates the Immigration and Nationality Act.

"At its core, this new rule is cruel: at a time when the cost of everything— from food to housing to healthcare — is unbearably high, immigrant families and U.S. citizen children will be punished for accessing these basic necessities," Rebecca Telzak, co-executive director of Make the Road New York, said in a statement.

Federal District Court Judge Ronnie Abrams of the Southern District of New York, an Obama appointee, set an initial conference for October 9 for the lawsuit brought by the states.

CNN's Gloria Pazmino contributed to this report.

For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com

articles.title: Young swing-state voters cozy up to Democratic Socialists, say party establishment must ‘learn’ from DSA wins
articles.summary: Young Michigan voters at Abdul El-Sayed's rally explain why Democratic Socialists of America's platform on Medicare for All appeals to them.
articles.body: Gen Z and young Millennial voters in Michigan who are leaning blue for the midterm election say they welcome the ideas of the Democratic Socialists of America, with a couple of voters agreeing that Americans should abolish the Senate. Fox News Digital was on the ground at Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed's "Students v. Billionaires" rally at Michigan State University on Sept. 11 and at the Detroit Health Department's annual block party, where young Democratic voters said rising costs and the complacency of the Democratic establishment have made the DSA more appealing to them. "I feel as if they actually focus on the people," said Detroit resident Shelby Campbell, who is also a 2023 Wayne State University graduate. "It's not as, I guess, capitalistic or just bought into the system. They want to do good, but they are just another big organization, and I think we just need to get rid of all the political parties and be independent." SHOCKING PERCENTAGE OF DEMOCRATS IDENTIFY AS 'DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' ACCORDING TO NEW POLL: 'TOXIC POLICIES' So far this election cycle, dozens of Democratic Socialists of America candidates have won their primary races, including Michigan state Rep. Donavan McKinney, who defeated incumbent Rep. Shri Thanedar, D-Mich. But some of the biggest upsets came out of New York, where New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a Democratic Socialists of America member, saw three candidates he endorsed — Claire Valdez, Darializa Avila Chevalier and Brad Lander — win their Democratic congressional primaries. The flurry of DSA-backed primary victories has put Republicans on the offensive while fueling concern among some Democrats about the socialist movement’s growing influence within the party. Noel Otteson is a sophomore at Michigan State University. He described himself as a "leftist" and "anti-capitalist," but he said he supports El-Sayed for his Medicare for All stance and his promise to get money out of politics. SCHUMER DODGES QUESTION ON WHETHER DSA BELONGS IN DEMOCRATIC PARTY "I believe in the power of people and democracy over corporations and oligarchs running everything, putting millions upon millions if not billions of dollars into Congress too," Otteson told Fox News Digital. "The system is rigged against the average person and is in favor of corporations and special interests and lobbyists," Otteson continued. Otteson said he supports the DSA's proposal to abolish the U.S. Senate, which he called "undemocratic." "The way that the Senate is set up is inherently undemocratic," Otteson said. "I'm someone who always, always, prioritizes democracy, and the Senate isn't that." "Some states hold more power than others based on population, and I would probably advocate for a more parliamentary system, you know, things like the U.K. and a lot of other European countries have, or most other countries have actually," Otteson said. NEWSOM ADMITS DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST IDEAS ‘MAINSTREAM’ IN DEMOCRAT PARTY: ‘PRETTY ALIGNED’ He proposed that the House of Representatives should be expanded. And in the heart of Detroit, Jahdante Smith, who is a Green Party candidate for District 9 of the Michigan House of Representatives, agreed that the Senate has got to go. "Their stance on abolishing the Senate, I think that is something that can work, only because the Senate is one of the most exclusionary clubs in politics and is also very, very hard to get into, and I think if you have a Republican and Democrat in the U.S. Senate in one state, they kind of cancel each other out, and they really don't get anything positive done," Smith told Fox News Digital. Smith said he supports the DSA's anti-ICE agenda and Medicare for All proposals, but wants to see the organization bring about actual change. "I support their ideas, but I love to see them have more traction in getting things actually done. Policy is something that you have to enact. It's not bills die in Congress, bills die on Capitol Hill every day," Smith told Fox News Digital. "You have to be able to get those bills passed through. I do support their stance on anti-ice." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Blake, a Michigan State University freshman, said he likes a lot of what the Democratic Socialists of America is pushing but said he's not on board with everything on its agenda, including abolishing the Senate. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The standard democrat has shown themselves to more or less be incapable of standing up for themselves and standing up for what's right," Blake told Fox News Digital. "So I've leaned on, I've decided to take my allegiances with further parties on more extreme sides of leftism because they can do what needs to be done." "And I feel like that's a lesson that normal Democrats need to learn," Blake continued.

articles.title: Trump’s authoritarian mindset can’t handle dissent from his appointees
articles.summary: Defiance from the supreme court and the Federal Reserve chair in one week... how ever will the US president cope?
articles.body:
"It's not personal, Sonny. It's strictly business," Michael Corleone tells his brother, Sonny, in The Godfather. But for Donald Trump , it's always personal. And he leaves this week feeling betrayed.

First, the US supreme court rejected his effort to restrict mail-in ballots ahead of the midterm elections. "These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court," the president wrote on his Truth Social platform. "They are merely a shell of their original selves."

Then the Federal Reserve defied Trump by raising its benchmark interest rate by a quarter-percentage point to a range of 3.75% to 4%, marking its first rate hike in three years. The Trump-appointed Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, described it as "a sober decision, serious decision, responsible decision".

The president lashed out again but was careful to blame the board rather than Warsh. Trump told reporters he had spoken to the chair. "I said you might ⁠as well vote with the board because it's not going to matter. The board is very hostile. They're very political."

It was an effort to rationalise a shock to the system for Trump, who instinctively assumes that anyone he appoints to high office will be eternally in his debt and automatically do his bidding. It is a view constantly reinforced by his cartoonishly loyal cabinet, from defence secretary Pete Hegseth to attorney general Todd Blanche , who was previously Trump's personal lawyer.

Blanche held a press conference in the White House Rose Garden on Tuesday and staunchly defended Trump. He was rewarded two days later when he attended a campaign rally in Gastonia , North Carolina, and heard Trump say of him: "He'll go down as the greatest attorney general in the history of our country."

But the supreme court is a different matter. Its conservative majority includes three justices appointed by Trump during his first term. It has certainly given him plenty of wins in emergency appeals during his second term, lifting lower court orders that had blocked his crackdown on immigration, ban on transgender people serving in the military and dismantling of the education department.

Perhaps that is why the defeats rankle and, to him, appear inexplicable. The justices struck down his far-reaching tariffs on nearly every other country and his restrictions on birthright citizenship while blocking his attempt to immediately fire Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook.

Last week, the court refused to allow Missouri to use new elections maps redrawn at Trump's urging to help Republicans gain an extra seat in the House of Representatives.

Then came this week's knockback of his administration's planned restrictions on mail-in voting, which Trump has long condemned as fraudulent while continuing to vote by mail himself. Of the nine-member court, only justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito dissented.

For the authoritarian mindset, this does not compute. Trump has become accustomed to snuffing out the first sparks of dissent among Republicans in Congress before the flames of rebellion can spread. He has taken a scythe to government departments and entities such as the Kennedy Center, which he is now threatening to demolish .

But not even he can control his own appointments when they serve in institutions protected by America's system of checks and balances. The irony is that they might be saving Trump from his own worst impulses. The Fed's intervention, for example, is aimed at curbing the rising prices that are hurting Trump politically. Warsh explained: "The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long."

It may only be a matter of time before Warsh's honeymoon period ends and he feels the president's wrath. But the Fed chair may also be aware that time is be on his side: every day brings Trump closer to the point at which Republicans begin looking beyond him to 2028.

Last weekend, Mike Johnson, the House speaker, said only that Congress will "debate and discuss" Trump's promise to give Americans $5,000 if Republicans retain control. On Thursday Maria Elvira Salazar, a Republican congresswoman from Florida, forcefully criticised the president's deportation agenda in a campaign ad.

Larry Jacobs , director of the Center for the Study of Politics and Governance at the University of Minnesota, says: "We're starting to see institutions like the supreme court and the Republicans in the Senate more consistently resisting him. This is the beginning of the lame duck session for Trump. This is the entry point for where it's going to be: a sour grapes moment in Trump's political career ."

articles.title: Judge isn't swayed by government's claims that plans for an 'anti-weaponization fund' are dead
articles.summary: A federal judge who blocked the creation of a $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization fund” for compensating President Donald Trump's political allies wasn't swayed...
articles.body:
ALEXANDRIA, Va. (AP) — A federal judge who blocked the creation of a $1.8 billion "anti-weaponization fund" for compensating President Donald Trump's political allies wasn't swayed by a government attorney's assurances Friday that the administration has abandoned the concept.

U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema in Virginia didn't rule from the bench on the government's request for her to dismiss a lawsuit challenging the fund's formation and operation. But the judge rejected the notion that the case's claims are moot because the Trump administration says the fund is dead and won't go forward.

"The issues that underlie this case are still alive and kicking, in my view," Brinkema said.

The fund for compensating Trump's political allies encountered a fierce bipartisan backlash and threatened to derail Attorney General Todd Blanche's Senate confirmation. On Aug. 2, Blanche issued a formal order terminating the fund after negotiating for weeks with two Republican senators who wanted to see the promise in writing before they endorsed his nomination.

"The case is moot," Justice Department attorney Andrew Block told Brinkema. "The mootness has been addressed at every stage."

But the judge noted that Blanche's assurances have been undercut by the president and other administration officials. Trump, a Republican, continued to publicly express support for the fund even as Blanche insisted it was dead.

"They contradict themselves all the time," Brinkema said.

The administration created the settlement fund to resolve Trump's lawsuit against the IRS over the leak of his tax returns. The plan stoked outrage over the notion that Trump supporters who attacked police officers while storming the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, could be eligible for payments.

Attorneys from the legal advocacy group Democracy Forward sued in May, asking the Alexandria, Virginia, court to suspend the fund's implementation temporarily and stop the Trump administration from disbursing any payouts. Plaintiffs' attorneys argued the government can't divert taxpayer money to a slush fund for enriching Trump's allies.

Brinkema, who was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Bill Clinton, agreed in June to extend an order blocking the fund until further notice from the court.

Democracy Forward attorney Pooja Boisture told the judge on Friday that the administration will most likely move forward with the fund — "either in its current iteration or a new one" — if her order is lifted.

The Virginia lawsuit's plaintiffs include a fired prosecutor and a college professor acquitted of assaulting federal agents at a protest. Also named as plaintiffs are the government watchdog Common Cause; the city of New Haven, Connecticut; and the National Abortion Federation, an association of abortion providers.

"This scheme is an unprecedented, unlawful, and corrupt attempt to manipulate the legal process and laws intended to prevent political interference to achieve benefits that President Trump and his political allies could not have obtained lawfully," the plaintiffs' attorneys wrote .

Justice Department attorneys argue the plaintiffs don't have a legal basis for claims challenging a fund that "has never existed and will not exist."

"The time has come to stop this inquisition," they wrote .

articles.title: ‘COVID 2.0’: Lawmakers push back on sweeping health 'police power' in key battleground state
articles.summary: Pennsylvania lawmakers told Fox News Digital the state's 502-page health code rewrite amounts to government overreach worse than COVID-era lockdowns.
articles.body: Pennsylvania lawmakers are warning that proposed changes to the state’s public health rules could usher in "COVID 2.0," giving health officials sweeping "police power" over residents during future disease outbreaks. Lawmakers opposing Pennsylvania's planned 502-page rewrite of state health code rules are urging the public to submit comments before the deadline, warning the proposal could serve as a roadmap to unfettered and intrusive restrictions and surveillance efforts, including the reported ability for agency representatives to enter private homes. "This absolutely is COVID 2.0, but it's even worse because [Governor] Josh Shapiro is trying to circumnavigate or skirt the constitutional provision that we the people in Pennsylvania voted to take that kind of power away from the governor," said state Rep. Russ Diamond, R-Lebanon, who is leading the charge against the policy changes. "We were the only state in the nation to reduce our governor's powers by a constitutional amendment after COVID," Diamond said, adding that "surveillance, segregation and quarantine" are areas being assessed. SOVIET-BORN ANALYST EXPOSES HOW PANDEMIC-ERA NEIGHBOR SNITCHING UNLOCKED A 'NATURE OF EVIL' IN AMERICA Pennsylvania voters approved a constitutional amendment in 2021 limiting the duration of a governor’s disaster declaration to 21 days unless extended by the General Assembly. Those emergency powers played a central role in then-Gov. Tom Wolf’s statewide mitigation orders. In the 502-page proposed Regulation 10-242, Communicable and Noncommunicable Diseases, the Pennsylvania Department of Health proposes expanding the list of reportable diseases, infections and conditions and updating the rules to reflect changing expert standards. "The Department proposes to add language in this subsection, indicating that the Department or a local health authority may enter an apartment, a building, a health care facility, a school, college or university, or other location as necessary to conduct its investigation under 208 this chapter," one provision highlighted by critics reads. "I don't think that we want a very left-leaning governor with his Department of Health and their henchmen having this kind of police power in Pennsylvania," Diamond said. A spokesperson for Health Secretary Dr. Debra Bogen — who led the Pittsburgh area’s COVID mitigation response — said Shapiro "did not personally propose" the updates and rejected critics’ characterizations. "Any misconstruing of these proposed changes designed to scare Pennsylvanians is inaccurate and disingenuous," Neil Ruhland told Fox News Digital. A Shapiro spokesperson also responded to criticism Wednesday, saying the governor’s philosophy is that "public health depends on trust" and emphasizing that the proposed health regulations are part of a larger effort to update about 200 regulatory areas across state agencies. Lapowsky told Fox News Digital that the public, stakeholders, independent regulators and the legislature can review and respond to the proposed changes. "Once public comment concludes later this month, [Shapiro] will weigh in, and the regulations will be revised accordingly," she said. Lapowsky said Shapiro’s emphasis on public trust includes respecting parental rights. Critics say the proposed regulations could give health officials greater authority over certain disease-control measures involving children, including masking. Lapowsky added that the governor believes "government should work closely with the people it serves." GOV SHAPIRO SUES TRUMP ADMINISTRATION OVER ‘LIFESAVING REPRODUCTIVE CARE’ IN ESCALATING ABORTION BATTLE Ruhland said the Pennsylvania Department of Health began analyzing and proposing regulatory updates several years ago and that the regulations in question are 25 years old and need modernization to "better support evolving public health needs and manage dangerous disease." While the proposed regulations do not themselves enact a new mask mandate, they would broaden disease-control language beyond "surveillance," a term central to litigation over Pennsylvania’s statewide school masking order during the pandemic. Pennsylvania House Minority Leader Jesse Topper told Fox News Digital that although the proposed regulations directly affect Pennsylvania, Americans elsewhere should also pay attention. "Everybody in the United States was impacted by COVID one way or another," said Topper, R-McConnellsburg. "We were one of the worst locked-down states in the entire nation. And we had one of the worst death rates from COVID… We don't want unelected bureaucrats making those decisions. We need to follow the [Commonwealth] Constitution, which says, ‘Hey, you can declare a public health disaster emergency if you want. But after 21 days, the legislature gets to say whether you can continue that or not’." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER State Sen. Doug Mastriano, R-Gettysburg, who, along with Diamond, led demonstrations against lockdown policies during COVID, told Fox News Digital that the proposed regulations are an "end-round" around voters. "Pennsylvania endured enough government overreach during COVID. We will not go back," said Mastriano, whom President Donald Trump nominated to serve as U.S. ambassador to Slovakia. Jason Richey, an attorney and the Republican nominee for lieutenant governor, also dubbed the changes "COVID 2.0." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "These are even worse than the COVID rules... [DOH] can look at your medical records. They can enter any building and go in without a warrant to do an investigation. They can even take your kid from school and talk to him privately without your consent," Richey said in a video recorded outside a Pennsylvania Department of Health office in Lehigh County last week. Beyond the public health implications, Topper said he is concerned that the proposed regulations would expand government authority. Topper and Ruhland both encouraged Pennsylvanians to submit feedback on the proposed regulations before Monday’s public-comment deadline.

articles.title: WATCH: Ilhan Omar denies feds have contacted her after border czar Homan confirms 'criminal' investigation
articles.summary: Tom Homan confirmed an ongoing criminal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, but the congresswoman says DHS has not contacted her about any probe.
articles.body: Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., told Fox News Digital she has not been made aware of any criminal investigation into her after White House border czar Tom Homan said Sunday that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is investigating allegations involving Omar. "No, they have not," Omar said after being asked if the DHS had reached out to her about any investigation. Homan confirmed that there is an "ongoing criminal investigation" into the Minnesota Democrat on "The Sunday Briefing." Homan declined to give comment on whether the federal government had evidence that Omar committed immigration or naturalization fraud — a popular allegation against Omar that has prompted numerous calls for a probe. Homan also declined to give specifics on what the investigation is centered on. HOMAN CONFIRMS 'CRIMINAL' INVESTIGATION INVOLVING ILHAN OMAR, SAYS HE KNOWS 'THINGS ARE GOING ON’ When asked directly whether Homan was confirming an investigation involving Omar, Homan replied, "I'm confirming that ICE is, yeah — look, I said months ago that there's something that's been reported and needs to be looked at." Fox News Digital asked Omar for her response to the allegations, particularly the claim that she married a man who critics allege is her brother as part of a scheme to obtain citizenship in the U.S. "The right wing has always had this s--- going, so I don't really worry about it," Omar said about the allegations. Omar has repeatedly denied claims that she married her brother, as well as claims that any investigation involving her has been opened by DHS or the Justice Department. There has been no public evidence available to confirm an open investigation into Omar. ILHAN OMAR NOT OUT OF THE WOODS DESPITE FINANCIAL DISCLOSURE REVISION, TOP REPUBLICAN WARNS Vice President JD Vance claimed in May that the Justice Department was looking into allegations against Omar — both related to the claim she married her brother and fraud after her amended financial disclosure forms and steep drop in net worth caught national attention. If we can prove it, that you shouldn't have been here in the first place, we will deport you," Mullin said on the podcast. Omar is a naturalized citizen, but Homan said there is a denaturalization process for cases of proven immigration fraud, which he claimed had been done "many times." "It’s a very serious process, so if someone lies through that process to become a citizen, and we can prove they, in fact, lied or misrepresented themselves, we can absolutely denaturalize them."

articles.title: Despite Senate Success, College Sports Bill Faces Uphill Battle in the House
articles.summary: "The stars have to align in the House for the bill to pass.”
articles.body:
The Protect College Sports Act (PCSA) is expected to easily pass the Senate after garnering overwhelming support during two procedural votes this week.

Once the bill passes the Senate, which could happen next week, lobbying machines both for and against the bill will turn their focus toward the House. But despite unprecedented bipartisan momentum, the PCSA faces an uphill battle in the House.

The roadblocks include a condensed timeline, Democratic opposition, potential Republican defectors, and perhaps even a tepid response from House Republican leadership, sources in and around Capitol Hill tell Front Office Sports. Given the slim Republican majority in the House, the bill likely can't afford to lose any Republicans—or may need to flip a few Democrats.

If the House can't get the bill to Trump's desk by the end of 2026, lawmakers would have to restart the entire legislative process next year.

"It's not dead by any stretch," one source tells FOS . "But the stars have to align in the House for the bill to pass."

The bill, first introduced by Sens.Ted Cruz (R., Texas), Maria Cantwell (D., Wash.), Eric Schmitt (R., Mo.) and Chris Coons (D., Del.) in May, seeks to double the revenue-sharing cap but implement NIL, transfer, and eligibility restrictions. It also provides protections for women's and Olympic sports at certain wealthy schools, offers the ability for schools to pool media rights to sell together in the future, and imposes rules around realignment and the football coaching carousel.

The first hurdle is time. The House won't return to session until after the November midterms, guaranteeing that the PCSA wouldn't be taken up until the "lame duck session" in between elections and the new Congress. That's a notoriously difficult period to pass any legislation. Multiple sources questioned the commitment of House Republican leadership to push the bill through the chamber.

Earlier this week, House Speaker Mike Johnson (R., La.) said he was interested in moving the legislation forward, but may want to make changes. Meanwhile, House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R., La.), could have concerns with the bill, one source said, given his allegiance to the SCORE Act (a much more partisan bill that offers more antitrust protections to the NCAA and prevents athletes from being deemed employees than the PCSA). A representative for Scalise didn't immediately respond to a comment request.

"I think they [Johnson and Scalise] want to get something done," Sen. Schmitt told FOS earlier this week. "We're going to work through timing and schedule and all those sorts of things, but I think people are generally very positive here." Schmitt confirmed discussions around potentially bringing the House back into session before the midterms, though that's up to Johnson.

Another issue House Republicans could contend with: defections from Florida House Republicans.

During Senate procedural votes, Florida Sens. Rick Scott and Ashley Moody voted against advancing the bill because of concerns from FSU and Miami over the conference realignment provisions, FOS previously reported . On Friday, both FSU and Miami released statements confirming their issues over the expansion provision and thanking the Florida senators. At least one Miami representative has said they will lean on Florida House members as well, a source familiar with the matter told FOS .

President Donald Trump may have something to say about the Republican defectors. Trump has voiced his support for the PCSA and has blessed members of his presidential committees Cody Campbell and Randy Levine, as well as others, to advocate for the bill on his behalf. Trump called Scott and Moody about their opposition to the bill, the aforementioned source said (in addition to calling them out in a Truth Social post).

"It remains to be seen how much pressure the President is willing to put on them, and how effective [the White House] can be," another source tells FOS .

Meanwhile, some House Democrats and left-leaning groups are expected to put up a big fight in the House to prevent any Democrats from voting yes.

The Congressional Black Caucus, which sources say has much more power in the House than in the Senate, has come out against the bill, as have the AFL-CIO and NAACP . In line with other CBC members, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D., N.Y.) has previously taken a strong stance against legislation supported by the SEC. Jeffries's office didn't immediately respond to a comment request.

Rep. Lori Trahan, (D., Mass.), could also put up a fight. Trahan has already proven her influence as one of the key representatives lobbying against the SCORE Act. She's expected to consider lobbying strategies against the PCSA in the coming weeks during the recess, a House aide said. "It's pretty tough," the first source said, "to fight against the [Congressional] Black Caucus and Lori Trahan."

articles.title: Swing state mayor sued as city’s Muslim holiday displays ignite religious-favoritism fight
articles.summary: A federal lawsuit alleges Dearborn spent thousands on Ramadan displays while Mayor Abdullah Hammoud stonewalled requests for Easter and Passover.
articles.body: A federal lawsuit filed Thursday alleges the city of Dearborn spent thousands of taxpayer dollars on public displays celebrating Muslim holidays while ignoring a Christian resident’s repeated requests for Easter and Passover recognition. Margot Cleveland, a journalist with The Federalist, filed a civil rights lawsuit with the American Freedom Law Center (AFLC) against the city of Dearborn and Democratic Mayor Abdullah Hammoud, alleging the city violated her First and Fourteenth Amendment rights, including protections involving religious establishment, free speech and equal protection. "The City of Dearborn spent taxpayer money to light up its streets and parks for Ramadan while stonewalling a resident who simply asked that Easter, Passover, and other Christian and Jewish holy days be treated the same way," Robert J. Muise, AFLC co-founder and senior counsel, said in a statement. "That is a straightforward Establishment Clause violation, and the retaliation our client faced for speaking up about it only compounds the constitutional harm." PASTOR UNLEASHES ON DEARBORN AS RELIGIOUS TENSIONS ERUPT AT CITY COUNCIL MEETING: 'ENOUGH IS ENOUGH' Dearborn is home to one of the largest Arab American communities in the country. The city had 109,976 residents in the 2020 Census, and 54.5% reported Middle Eastern or North African ancestry. Michigan Avenue, the city’s main thoroughfare, is lined with businesses featuring Arabic-script signs and Middle Eastern cuisine. There are ten mosques within the city limits, according to an online directory. Hammoud was first elected mayor in November 2021, becoming the first Muslim and Arab American to lead the city of Dearborn. "What makes this case especially troubling is that City officials, up to and including the Mayor, responded to a citizen’s respectful request for equal treatment with silence, stonewalling, and outright hostility — including the Mayor’s own words telling a Christian resident he is ‘not welcome’ in his own city," David Yerushalmi, an attorney on the case, said. "Our client is simply asking the City to treat Christians and Jews as equal citizens." Lawyers for Cleveland pointed to a September exchange between Hammoud and Christian pastor Ted Barham as evidence of what they allege is the city’s hostility toward Christians. Barham had raised concerns during a City Council meeting over the city’s decision to rename a street after Usama Siblani, publisher of The Arab American News, who has made statements expressing support for Hezbollah. TRUMP INAUGURATION PASTOR SAYS DEARBORN CHRISTIANS 'AFRAID' TO SPEAK OUT IN MUSLIM-MAJORITY CITY In the exchange, Hammoud called Barham a "bigot" and an "Islamaophobe." "And although you live here, I want you to know as mayor, you are not welcome here," Hammoud told the Christian pastor. "And the day you move out of the city will be the day that I launch a parade celebrating the fact that you moved out of the city . . . because you are not somebody who believes in coexistence." But Cleveland’s lawsuit alleges that city leaders ignored her requests for the city to also recognize Christian and Jewish holidays after she began seeing "Ramadan Kareem" banners and large crescent moons displayed across the city in spring 2025. A FOIA request revealed that the city had spent $1,500 on Ramadan banners and $5,000 on the crescent-moon display. The Dearborn Police Department was also selling Ramadan-themed T-shirts. In emails to the city, Cleveland said she did not want the city to stop celebrating Muslim holidays but wanted equal recognition for Christian and Jewish holy days. "I much prefer to ensure equality of faith traditions, as opposed to a challenge to the display," Cleveland wrote in an email. MASSACHUSETTS HIGH COURT BLOCKS CITY FROM DISPLAYING CATHOLIC SAINT STATUES HONORING FIRST RESPONDERS Not only did the city allegedly ignore Cleveland’s requests, but in February 2026, it expanded its Ramadan displays, commissioning crescent-and-star lights that were displayed on municipal streetlights across the city. "This initiative reflects who we are as a city," Hammoud said in a statement. Tensions between Cleveland and city officials continued in April, when Cleveland alleges she was told she could attend a community meeting as a resident but not as a journalist. The lawsuit also alleges Hammoud made what it describes as a "snide comment" about residents who criticize the city on social media to monetize their posts. The lawsuit also alleges that in February 2026, the city expanded its Ramadan displays, commissioning crescent-and-star lights for municipal streetlights across the city. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Cleveland pushed back, according to the lawsuit, saying she was simply "a concerned resident who was ignored when I asked for the City to treat Christians and Jews equally." "Despite the repeated requests, they treated her as if she were an outsider and not a full member of the political community," Muise told Fox News Digital. The lawsuit comes during Michigan’s closely watched 2026 U.S. Senate race, with Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, who is Muslim and the son of Egyptian immigrants, facing Republican nominee Mike Rogers for the state’s open Senate seat. Religion and antisemitism have become points of dispute in the race, with Republicans and some Democrats criticizing El-Sayed over his association with streamer Hasan Piker, who said the U.S. was worse than al Qaeda "pound for pound, as far as the number of deaths," while arguing that U.S. military actions that kill civilians can amount to acts of terror. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP At the same time, El-Sayed and his supporters have accused opponents of targeting him with anti-Muslim rhetoric. Fox News Digital reached out to Hammoud’s office and Cleveland’s attorneys for comment.

articles.title: How CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin's family foundation became a major funder of left-wing activist groups
articles.summary: Arc of Justice, the family foundation tied to CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin, provided nearly $3.2 million to the protest group since 2009.
articles.body: CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin's family foundation became a major financial backer of a network of left-wing activist organizations over more than two decades, providing nearly $3.2 million to CodePink while also bankrolling protest groups, legal advocacy organizations and progressive nonprofits, a Fox News Digital investigation found. The foundation, Arc of Justice, is a $54.6 million private foundation formerly known as The Benjamin Fund. A review of its complete IRS filing history found it made nearly 1,500 grants totaling about $24.6 million to organizations involved in anti-war activism, progressive policy, legal advocacy and campaigns involving immigration enforcement, China, Cuba and the Israel-Hamas war. Among its largest recipients were CodePink, Global Exchange, the Center for Constitutional Rights, Grassroots International and Social Good Fund, alongside grants to dozens of other organizations involved in anti-war activism, progressive policy, legal advocacy and progressive media. Arc of Justice provided CodePink more than twice the approximately $1.33 million the group received from the funding network linked to Shanghai-based Marxist tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham. A previous five-part Fox News Digital investigation found Singham's network directed at least $278 million into organizations that promoted pro-China messaging. LAWMAKERS THROW OUT 'TROJAN HORSE' ACTIVISTS THEY SAY ARE ENGAGED IN AMERICAN SUBVERSION Arc of Justice has come under scrutiny after California revoked its charitable registration following years of financial compliance failures, though the foundation has been working to regain its standing with California regulators. Benjamin, who co-founded CodePink with Singham’s wife Jodie Evans, has remained one of the group's most visible public faces, frequently leading protests and interrupting congressional hearings. On Tuesday, she was escorted from a House Foreign Affairs subcommittee hearing on alleged foreign malign influence after protesting during the proceedings. The Fox News Digital investigation also found the foundation itself has undergone sweeping changes in recent months, with Benjamin stepping down from the board, new leadership taking over and the organization saying it intends to chart a different course for its charitable giving. Following the money Arc of Justice began funding CodePink in 2009 and provided grants to the organization in 15 tax years through 2024, totaling $3,195,280. According to the documents, CodePink was Arc of Justice's largest activist beneficiary. Since 2009, the foundation and its predecessor, The Benjamin Fund, also directed about $2.05 million to Global Exchange, the anti-war and social justice advocacy group Benjamin co-founded with her former husband, Kevin Danaher, which has long campaigned against U.S. military intervention and economic sanctions. Arc of Justice also provided about $2.24 million to Grassroots International, which funds grassroots social movements around the world; $1.61 million to Social Good Fund, which provides nonprofit infrastructure and fundraising support for charitable projects; about $1.29 million to the Center for Constitutional Rights, a legal advocacy organization; and about $114,000 to Alliance for Global Justice (AFGJ), an activist nonprofit. AFGJ has drawn scrutiny over its past fiscal sponsorship of Samidoun, a pro-Palestinian activist group later sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury. Benjamin said Arc's final grant to Alliance for Global Justice was $10,000 in 2022 and that the foundation "was not aware of any specific groups fiscally sponsored by AFGJ" when it made its grants. Through attorney David Levitt, the foundation said both CodePink and Alliance for Global Justice were recognized by the IRS as tax-exempt public charities and that Arc was entitled to rely on that status when making its grants. The grantmaking reached across a much broader activist network. Since 2009, IRS filings reviewed by Fox News Digital show Arc of Justice and its predecessor gave about $492,000 to World Beyond War, roughly $255,000 to the Institute for Policy Studies and about $124,000 to Jewish Voice for Peace. It also gave $110,000 to Grassroots Global Justice and about $90,000 to the Center for Popular Democracy. IRS filings also show Arc of Justice and its predecessor provided about $65,500 to Democracy Now! since 2009, where Benjamin has frequently appeared as a guest over the years. WATCH: CodePink activists questioned on motives ahead of foreign influence hearing From funding to activism Founded in 2002 with the aim of preventing the Iraq War, CodePink has grown into one of the country's most visible anti-war protest groups, repeatedly disrupting congressional hearings and protests involving senior U.S. officials, including then-Secretaries of State John Kerry and Mike Pompeo. The group has also participated in nationwide No Kings protests, opposed ICE enforcement actions, organized anti-Israel rallies and campaigned against U.S. policy toward China, Cuba and Iran. Earlier this year, CodePink led a delegation to Cuba that included Twitch political streamer Hasan Piker. Asked about Arc's long-term funding of CodePink and other activist organizations, Matthew Johnson, a senior fellow at the Jamestown Foundation, said sustained financial support can have an impact well beyond the dollar amounts involved. "Small amounts of money can actually go a long way toward impacting the broader media ecosystem... from the perspective of political organization, they may be having an outsized impact on the kind of information that is available to Americans," Johnson told Fox News Digital. Johnson, who testified before Congress Tuesday about how foreign adversaries may use nonprofits and other organizations to shape U.S. public opinion and policy, told lawmakers that CodePink launched its "China Is Not Our Enemy" campaign in 2020 following meetings in Beijing and has since pursued China-focused advocacy and organized travel. The campaign argued the United States should pursue cooperation with Beijing rather than confrontation. CodePink and Benjamin have denied taking direction from the Chinese government. WATCH: Heritage Foundation senior fellow confronts CodePink's Medea Benjamin before House hearing Benjamin told Fox News Digital the grants were intended to support CodePink's anti-war work. "The foundation's donations to CodePink were made to support its anti-war work," she said in an email response. At the House hearing on Tuesday, Benjamin also rejected suggestions that she or CodePink took direction from foreign governments. "I've been an anti-war activist from the days of Vietnam," Benjamin said. "I never had a foreign government tell me what to do." Singham and the organizations he has funded, identified in the Fox News Digital report, have denied taking direction from the Chinese government, and neither Singham, Benjamin nor the organizations have been charged with wrongdoing. CHINA EXPERT WARNS BEIJING WANTS AMERICANS — NOT THE CCP — TO SPREAD ITS MESSAGE Where did the money come from? Arc of Justice was formerly known as The Benjamin Fund, Inc., with California corporate records showing the foundation formally changed its name in November 2019. Benjamin's father, Alvin Benjamin, a prominent Long Island real estate developer who founded The Benjamin Companies in the early 1960s, provided some of the foundation's earliest documented financial backing. The Benjamin Fund's initial 2003 IRS return shows he contributed a partnership interest valued at $683,715 to the foundation, with Medea Susan Benjamin serving as president. Much larger contributions followed. In 2010, the estate of Benjamin's mother, Rose Benjamin, contributed $10,863,060, according to the foundation's IRS filing. Five years later, the Estate of Alvin Benjamin contributed another $15 million, followed by another $8,603,450 in 2019. Medea Benjamin — identified as Susan Benjamin on the filing — personally contributed $1 million to Arc of Justice in 2022, listing a Miami address. How the fortune grew Arc of Justice's wealth was largely tied to an investment portfolio that continued to grow while the foundation distributed millions of dollars in grants. Federal tax returns reviewed by Fox News Digital show the foundation's assets grew from $39.63 million at the end of 2020 to $54.64 million in 2024, as it distributed millions of dollars annually in grants. Arc of Justice generated much of its annual income from its investment portfolio, collecting dividends from stocks and mutual funds, interest on cash holdings and profits from investments that had increased in value. In 2023, the foundation reported nearly $2 million in revenue, including $1.11 million in dividends and interest from securities, $166,421 in interest on savings and temporary cash investments and $686,919 in net gains from asset sales. Its investment holdings also produced substantial gains as the portfolio increased in value. In 2020, Arc of Justice reported $12,344,501 in unrealized gains on securities, helping push its year-end assets to nearly $40 million. Over more than two decades, IRS filings reviewed by Fox News Digital repeatedly reported no compensation for the foundation's officers and no highly paid employees, while the foundation directed millions of dollars to outside organizations. Changing course After California revoked Arc of Justice's charitable registration, Fox News Digital reported that a new Florida nonprofit using the Arc of Justice name was incorporated at the Miami home of Benjamin's longtime partner, Tighe Barry, raising questions about the future of the foundation and whether its assets or operations were being moved out of California. The address is a modest turquoise home largely obscured by trees — an unassuming setting for an organization tied to a private foundation with more than $50 million in assets. Benjamin and Barry have frequently appeared together at CodePink demonstrations over the years. Levitt later told Fox News Digital the Florida corporation had been created as a "placeholder" while the foundation considered relocating its operations from California, but the move was never completed. He said the California corporation was never formally dissolved, no assets were transferred and the Florida entity "holds no assets and has conducted no business." The foundation has been attempting to get its registration reinstated after recently filing five years of overdue reports covering 2020 through 2024 and paying $1,800 in filing fees and penalties as part of a petition for reinstatement, documents submitted to California regulators show. $54M CODEPINK-LINKED FOUNDATION SHUT DOWN IN CALIFORNIA POPS UP AT RAMSHACKLE MIAMI HOME In the reinstatement petition, Levitt attributed the missed filings to what he described as an administrative misunderstanding over whether the foundation had successfully relocated from California to Florida. He wrote that, during the tenure of the foundation's "former president," who served through the end of 2025, foundation leaders believed Arc was no longer subject to California's charitable registration requirements because it had moved to Florida. The petition says the foundation later appointed a "new president," who discovered the compliance problems in 2026 and began the process of bringing the organization back into compliance. The petition also states that the foundation's directors and officers personally paid the penalty portion of the overdue filing fees. The filings identify Maya Danaher, Benjamin's daughter, as president of the California foundation. Danaher previously served as the foundation's treasurer before becoming president. "As previously reported, I have resigned from the foundation's board, and its new management will set its own funding priorities going forward," Benjamin said. LAWMAKERS SAY THEY ARE STANDING AT THE GATES AGAINST 'TROJAN HORSES' PROMOTING MALIGN FOREIGN INTERESTS It is unclear why Benjamin resigned from the board, why the proposed move to Florida was ultimately abandoned or why the foundation's new leadership decided to shift its grantmaking priorities away from the causes it had supported for more than two decades. Benjamin was not listed as an officer or director of the Florida corporation, where Barry was listed as secretary and registered agent. Its stated goal is blunt: "WE ARE HERE TO SUPPORT SOCIAL JUSTICE NON PROFITS," according to the articles of incorporation. "Going forward, the foundation's new management intends to focus its grant-making on domestic childhood enrichment programs and organizations that support the well-being of children, families and individuals in need throughout the U.S.," Levitt said. articles.title: Judge strikes down Trump administration’s $600 million in cuts to teacher training
articles.summary: A federal judge on Thursday struck down a 2025 order from the Trump administration that cut hundreds of millions of dollars in teacher training money.
articles.body: BOSTON — A federal judge on Thursday struck down a 2025 order from the Trump administration that cut hundreds of millions of dollars in teacher training money. U.S. District Judge Angel Kelley in Massachusetts wrote in her order that the Education Department’s directive violated federal law and was arbitrary and capricious. In February 2025, the Education Department cut about $600 million in grants for teacher training, characterizing them as supporting “divisive ideologies” such as diversity, equity and inclusion efforts. The grants were intended to address teacher shortages. The Education Department’s order was hasty, Kelley wrote. The administration did not follow requirements in the law for giving notice or accepting comments about a proposal, she said. She said they also didn’t take into account just how much the states and a wide array of students, teachers and principals rely on these grants. “In short, the reliance interests are many, substantial, and deep-rooted,” Kelley wrote. Her ruling does not restore the grant money. She writes that arguments related to recovering that funding need to be brought in the Court of Federal Claims. The Education Department did not immediately respond to an email from The Associated Press requesting comment. The directive had stripped the majority of funding to the Teacher Quality Partnership and Supporting Effective Educator Development, effecting more than 100 programs. Eight Democratic-led states sued, saying the cuts were likely driven by efforts from the Trump administration to eliminate diversity, equity and inclusion programs, and a federal judge in Boston temporarily halted the cuts. The federal appeals court in Boston turned away an appeal from the administration to allow them to resume. But in April 2025, the Supreme Court ruled the government could cut the grants while the case proceeds. The high court’s conservative majority wrote states could keep the programs running with their own money for now, despite the judge in Boston saying that the programs already were being effected. The states have argued that the grants help develop teachers in crucial areas such as math, science and special education, and that data has shown they help to boost teacher retention rates and ensure educators remain in the profession beyond five years.

articles.title: Dems abandon candidate who said MAGA is 'more destructive' than Nazis, but she’s stuck on the ballot
articles.summary: North Carolina Democrat Shelly Headen called for an attack on U.S. soil targeting red states and compared Trump to Hitler in resurfaced posts.
articles.body: A Democrat running for the state legislature in battleground North Carolina remains on the ballot despite her party publicly abandoning her after inflammatory social media posts she made resurfaced. The North Carolina House Democratic Caucus and a county party group both condemned posts by Shelly Headen in which the legislative candidate called for an attack on U.S. soil targeting red states and compared President Donald Trump to Adolf Hitler. But Headen remains a candidate because the filing deadline to drop out of the race was Aug. 20, and the general election ballots are finalized and were sent out to voters starting on Sept. 4. Headen, who is challenging Republican state Rep. John Blust for the House District 62 seat in Greensboro-anchored Guilford County, posted a year ago, "I think our only hope is an attack on US Soil … preferably Alabama, Louisiana … where the stupid people live." WATCH: HUGH HEWITT'S TAKE ON THE HEADEN CONTROVERSY In separate posts, she argued that the damage done by Trump was "getting close to surpassing Hitler" and claimed the "MAGA cult may be more destructive and evil than the Nazis." Breitbart reported that a Facebook post by Headen that pictured her at a memorial at the Nazis' Dachau concentration camp in Germany, where tens of thousands of people were murdered during World War II, with the words, "This is where Trump supporters belong." Headen denied last week to the Greensboro News and Record that she posted the concentration camp image and said she believed the image was edited to include the words over a real photo. Her old comments grabbed new national attention earlier this week when the White House Rapid Response account that supports Trump shared them on X and charged that Democrats "ARE SICK PEOPLE!" DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB North Carolina Republican U.S. Senate nominee Michael Whatley posted on social media a photo of Headen and former Gov. Roy Cooper, the Democratic Senate nominee, and argued, "Roy Cooper still stands with NC Dem who called for the genocide of Republicans. This is against everything America stands for." "These remarks are reprehensible – Roy strongly condemns them and all forms of political violence and he believes it’s up to all of us to speak responsibly," Cooper's campaign emphasized in a statement. Headen, a certified public accountant and small business owner, told WFDD, a public radio station in North Carolina, that she didn't remember making the posts but apologized to those hurt by them. And she added that she understood the party’s decision to drop support for her. But in an interview with The Assembly, a digital-first news operation in North Carolina, Headen defended her posts, describing them as "a few angry moments." "I’ve sacrificed myself just like Jesus sacrificed Himself on the cross, and Martin Luther King and Abraham Lincoln and all the people that put themselves out there to sacrifice for our country," Headen also told The Assembly. "If a few angry moments on social media are the end, then so be it. MAGA will keep winning if we continue with not standing up for what’s right." The Assembly's reporting preceded the move by Democrats to drop support. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "Shelly Headen’s posts are unacceptable and do not reflect the values we expect of our candidates," the North Carolina House Democratic Caucus said in a statement. The caucus added that it "condemns these comments without qualification and will not support Shelly Headen’s candidacy." The Guilford County Democratic Party said in a statement, "We unequivocally reject and condemn the social media posts by Shelly Headen. These statements violate everything our party represents. Effective immediately, the county Democratic Party is formally withdrawing all financial, operational and organizational support for Shelley Headen’s campaign." Headen earlier this week told Fox News Digital she's received death threats in recent days but declined to give any further responses regarding her posts. In an article published Thursday in The Rhino Times, Headen reiterated, "I’ve been getting death threats, and now all I want to do is protect myself and my family. My whole world has been collapsing." And she acknowledged that she took down her social media pages, saying, "I don’t have access to any of my accounts anymore." Republicans have spotlighted the controversy. North Carolina House Speaker Destin Hall called Headen's comments "Absolutely disgusting." And the North Carolina House Republicans wrote on X, "Democrat Shelly Headen who is "Running to Restore Human Decency" just posted that she wants an attack on US soil. It is unclear whether Shelly would prefer ISIS or China to attack the United States, but it’s clear she wants an attack." Meanwhile, the popular conservative X account Libs of TikTok argued that Headen "should drop out immediately. She doesn’t belong anywhere public office." The attention over the resurfaced comments comes a week after Headen faced a separate controversy following a move by State House Republicans to release two 2024 Guilford County Sheriff's Office incident reports involving her and her husband, Gregory Thomas Headen. The reports, which identify the alleged domestic offense as physical assault, list Headen as the suspect and her husband as the potential victim. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In a statement she released earlier this month, Headen said that during a stressful time in their marriage, she and her husband had "a couple of arguments that escalated." She said that, during one argument, her husband grabbed her, causing her to fall backward and hit her head. She then called 911. Headen, in her statement, described herself as having experienced abuse. And she argued that Republicans were using a private family matter for political gain.

articles.title: Socialist Claire Valdez faces calls for federal probe after Mexico ‘fight’ pledge
articles.summary: New York City socialist Claire Valdez faces Logan Act scrutiny after meeting Mexico's Morena party and vowing to carry independence fight to Congress.
articles.body: A New York City socialist seeking to replace a retiring Democrat drew criticism Thursday after pledging to carry the "fight" inspired by Mexico’s struggle for independence into Congress. And critics pointed to her disclosure that she met with members of Mexico’s ruling left-wing party. Claire Valdez, who is seeking Rep. Nydia Velázquez's seat in a district that includes Bushwick and Ridgewood, is facing calls for the State Department to investigate her under the Logan Act. It's a rarely enforced 1799 law that criminalizes certain unauthorized efforts by private citizens to influence foreign governments in disputes involving the U.S. Democrats have also invoked the law in connection with President Donald Trump. In response to her post, immigration attorney and columnist Alicia Nieves tweeted at Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, a former ambassador to Mexico, calling for an investigation of Valdez after the candidate disclosed that she had met with members of Morena, Mexico’s ruling left-wing party. "Given that she is currently a congressional nominee, not a member of Congress, and appears to have discussed facilitating support contrary to current U.S. policy as well as describing our country an ‘empire’ that has ‘stolen from us’ … I hope the administration will review whether these communications warrant investigation under the Logan Act." COLORADO'S SOCIALIST CANDIDATE CALLS FOR 'MORE IMMIGRANTS INTO OFFICE' TO STOP AMERICA'S 'EXPLOITATIVE' NATURE The act, enacted in 1799, came after the John Adams administration and congressional Federalists objected to Pennsylvania politician George Logan’s unauthorized trip to France, where he sought to ease tensions during what was called the "Quasi-War." Federalists feared private diplomacy could undermine the U.S. government’s foreign policy. Adams and his Federalist allies also viewed Logan’s actions through the partisan tensions surrounding the 1800 presidential race against Thomas Jefferson. In her tweet, Valdez wrote, "215 years ago, Mexicans fought an empire that demanded our land and our labor. And we won. "I'll carry that fight with me to Congress as New York's first Mexican-American representative," Valdez pledged. "And I'm strengthened not just by Mexico's history but its present." She said she met "comrades" in the Morena party who are "standing up to the empires and corporations that have always taken from us — and building a government for the working class. Viva la Independencia, Viva México!" MAMDANI-BACKED SOCIALIST PREVAILS IN CROWDED PRIMARY TO REPLACE RETIRING REP Fox News Digital reached out to Valdez and the Mexican government for comment. Morena could not immediately be reached. Critics also pointed out that Valdez's father, Larry, is linked to a company that helped construct a Texas immigration center during the Obama administration. They contended that the connection conflicts with her opposition to immigration enforcement. "This would be a great campaign for Congress in Mexico," added Christina Pushaw, a top communications official for Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis. Fox News Digital also reached out to community organizer Melvin Rivera, the Republican opponent facing Valdez, for comment. Democrats cited the Logan Act in connection with Trump after he publicly remarked, "Russia, if you’re listening, I hope you’re able to find the 30,000 emails that are missing" in reference to his 2016 opponent Hillary Clinton. Then-Senate Democratic Leader Harry Reid of Nevada suggested that Trump had violated the Logan Act. The law has also been invoked against other public figures, including former Sen. John Kerry, D-Mass., and the Rev. Jesse Jackson, but no prosecution under the statute has resulted in a conviction. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Two men faced proceedings under the Logan Act but were never convicted. A grand jury indicted Kentucky farmer Francis Flournoy in 1803 after he advocated a separate Western United States allied with France. Jonas P. Levy was arrested and held to bail under the law in 1853 after writing to Mexico’s president. articles.title: Vance ends Iowa rally with 7-minute censure of Rob Sand
articles.summary: Vice President Vance zeroed in on Iowa Democratic gubernatorial nominee Rob Sand during a rally in Council Bluffs on Friday, saying he is too far left to lead the state. Sand is leading in several polls in the contest to succeed Gov. Kim Reynolds (R) in November. In a roughly seven-minute attack on Sand, Vance…
articles.body:
Vice President Vance zeroed in on Iowa Democratic gubernatorial nominee Rob Sand during a rally in Council Bluffs on Friday, saying he is too far left to lead the state.

Sand is leading in several polls in the contest to succeed Gov. Kim Reynolds (R) in November.

In a roughly seven-minute attack on Sand, Vance accused the candidate of masquerading as a moderate when he is “far left.”

“He wants to make sure you hear him groaning about partisanship,” Vance told a crowd of supporters.

“He’ll say ‘Why do we even need labels’; that’s what he says. But it’s a strange thing to complain about from a guy who has spent his entire life working for and donating to far left, Democratic causes. If partisanship is a problem, and it is, the first place is to look in the damn mirror, Rob, because you’ve been a partisan Democrat your whole life,” he said.

Vance went on to hit Sand, who is the state’s auditor, on a number of fronts, including transgender people in women’s sports, abortion and the Green New Deal; and he sought to paint Sand and other Democratic candidates as extreme.

“The choice is this simple: It’s common sense versus crazy. It’s a man who listens to you versus a man who looks down on you. It’s a governor who fights for you versus a governor who fights against you,” Vance said.

“You have an opportunity to not send not just Rob Sand but the entire Democrat Party a message: Check the crazy at the door, and learn to fight for Americans for a change,” he continued.

Polls show a tight gubernatorial race potentially favoring Democrats in the Hawkeye State. A poll released earlier this month from Emerson College Polling/Nexstar Media shows Sand leading his Republican opponent Zach Lahn 49 percent to 46 percent.

Vance notably called out Kansas Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton and Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico at the rally. The comments come as polls show a tightening Senate race in Kansas.

While Lahn was present at the rally with Vance, one Iowa candidate who was noticeably absent was Republican Senate nominee Rep. Ashley Hinson.

The congresswoman’s Senate campaign said ahead of the rally that she had conflicting events. Hinson is facing a highly competitive race against Iowa state Rep. Josh Turek. The same Emerson College Polling/Nexstar Media survey showed Turek leading Hinson 46 percent to 44 percent.

“I know she couldn’t be here today, but are we going to elect Ashley Hinson for United States senator from the great state of Iowa?” the vice president said.

articles.title: Judge says issues in Trump administration anti-weaponization case 'alive and kicking' despite DOJ push
articles.summary: Judge Brinkema questioned whether the Trump administration's Anti-Weaponization Fund truly died or if the DOJ Judgment Fund serves as its equivalent.
articles.body: ALEXANDRIA, Va. — Department of Justice lawyers have asked U.S. District Court Judge Leonie Brinkema to dismiss a case connected to the Trump administration's $1.776 billion "Anti-Weaponization Fund," arguing that Attorney General Todd Blanche issued a formal recission order in August and has affirmed many times, including under oath before Congress, that the fund is dead. However, Brinkema seemed skeptical Friday. "The issues that underlie this case are still alive and kicking in my view," Brinkema said. "The real concern that lurks ... is the concept of taxpayer money being used to promote particular political views," Brinkema said, pointing to pro-life activists convicted of violating the FACE Act and others who attempted an "insurrection" on Jan. 6 "to overthrow the legitimate election." CLINTON JUDGE INDEFINITELY BLOCKS TRUMP'S $1.776B ANTI-WEAPONIZATION FUND "That entity is gone," said Brinkema, referring to the Anti-Weaponization Fund and agreeing that Blanche has said under oath at his confirmation hearings that the fund is dead. "But is there a functional equivalent?" Brinkema said, referring to the DOJ's ordinary Judgment Fund authority. The Judgment Fund is a permanent U.S. Treasury account managed by the Bureau of the Fiscal Service that pays court judgments and DOJ legal settlements against the federal government. Brinkema called that fund "a less transparent structure" and suggested that some defendants convicted of FACE Act crimes have already received large payouts from the DOJ's Judgment Fund. JUDGE TEMPORARILY BLOCKS TRUMP DOJ'S NEARLY $2B 'ANTI-WEAPONIZATION' FUND Here, Brinkema affirmed she was talking about the case of Paul Vaughn. Vaugh, of Centerville, Tennessee, was convicted in January 2024 for his role in blockading an abortion clinic in Mount Juliet, Tennessee, in March 2021. Vaughn ultimately received a pardon and a taxpayer-funded payout from the DOJ's Judgment Fund that confirmed to Fox News is "seven figures." BIDEN ADMIN USED ABORTION GROUP DOSSIERS, INCLUDING PHOTOS OF MINORS, TO TARGET CHRISTIANS, DOJ REPORT REVEALS DOJ lawyer Andrew Block asked what remedy the plaintiff wants, given "the fund is dead." Brinkema countered that although the case is nowhere near the remedy stage, "I think there are remedies." She brought up the possibility of requiring a "neutral" person to oversee a fund, "not someone from the DOJ, which I see unfortunately as coerced" in this matter. "A proper, unbiased look. ... There's been too much talk from members of the administration, which undercut [DOJ's] position," Brinkema said. "They contradict themselves all the time." articles.title: Wendy’s franchisee with hundreds of locations across 15 states files for bankruptcy
articles.summary: A Wendy’s franchisee that operates 314 of the fast food company’s restaurants in 15 states announced Friday that it will be filing for bankruptcy.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – A Wendy’s franchisee that operates 314 of the fast food company’s restaurants in 15 states announced Friday that it will be filing for bankruptcy.

Meritage Hospitality Group, headquartered in Grand Rapids, Michigan, announced in a news release that it was voluntarily filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in a bid to, in part, “strengthen its balance sheet.”

The news comes months after the company announced it would close 60 locations to boost its performance in 2026.

Meritage also owns one Bojangles and five “independently branded concepts,” but those ventures were not enough to offset the financial struggles of its Wendy’s stores.

“Because the substantial majority of Meritage’s restaurant portfolio operates under Wendy’s brand, those system-wide pressures have had a significant impact on the Company’s financial position,” the company said in the release.

Amid soaring beef costs , Wendy’s has reported same-store sales losses for six straight quarters, CNBC reports.

Meritage owns Wendy’s locations in Arkansas, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Indiana, Massachusetts, Michigan, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Texas, and Virginia.

The company, which made no mention of any closure plans, says it anticipates maintaining normal restaurant operations during the restructuring process, and “will continue to serve guests every day, and its team members remain the heart of this business.”

Nexstar reached out to Wendy’s corporate team for a statement, but did not immediately receive a response.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy holdout juror believed she was guilty ‘from day one,’ didn’t have any doubts
articles.summary: “He felt that she was sane when she did it. And that’s exactly what he told me,” Marcel recalled.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — The lone juror whose vote resulted in a mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy murder case says statements made about him by other jurors are not accurate.

Jury foreperson Roni Carlson told NBC 10 Boston that the holdout juror, Michael Desronvil, “admitted he had reasonable doubt” but allegedly refused to engage with the other jurors as to why. Carlson believed Desronvil was not properly applying the judge’s instructions on reasonable doubt and sent the judge a note raising her concerns.

Other jurors also alleged that Desronvil was dismissive of their arguments.

In a statement to NewsNation, he refuted the claims made by fellow jurors.

“I didn’t have any doubts,” the juror said. “As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence present. Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses, and what the prosecution presents, I thought it was enough proof that she (Clancy) knew exactly what she was doing and planned.”

Desronvil also spoke Tuesday in an interview with Ray Marcel on the streaming series “Fugitive TV.” Marcel told NewsNation’s Chris Cuomo on Wednesday that the lone juror believed Clancy was guilty from the beginning of the trial.

“He felt that she was sane when she did it. And that’s exactly what he told me,” Marcel recalled. “He said, from day one, that he always felt that she was guilty, and he never displayed or said anything about reasonable doubt.”

“He said things got heated in the jury room,” he continued. “Jurors were not agreeing, some agreeing, some not agreeing…. What he told me was, from day one, they voted every single day.”

Clancy’s defense attorney, Kevin Reddington , asked Judge William Sullivan to remove Desronvil from the jury, arguing that he was not following the law regarding reasonable doubt. The judge denied the request, and deliberations continued.

Holdout juror: Clancy prepared before kids’ deaths

Desronvil said that on the first day of deliberations, eight jurors believed Clancy was not guilty by reason of insanity.

By the end, only he and one other juror still believed she was guilty.

“And then, he said, at the last moment, that other juror decided to go not guilty, and he just stood his ground… He felt that she was sane by the preparation she did,” Marcel explained. “The preparation showed that she was sane and knew what she was doing, pretty much knew right from wrong, before she did what she did.”

He added that the public reaction after the trial was unreasonable. Since the mistrial, Desronvil has been publicly revealed as the holdout juror, had his address and phone number doxxed, and has received death threats.

Edward Andrew Paltzik, a leading defamation and media law attorney, announced Thursday that he is representing Desronvil.

“No matter if you agree with him or not… his name shouldn’t have been put out there like that,” Marcel told Cuomo. “No juror should be put to the forefront like that, because it’s their civic duty to do that, and they should be protected… He never asked for any of this whatsoever.”

NewsNation’s Steph Whiteside and Allison Hope Weiner contributed to this article.
