articles.title: California Gov. Gavin Newsom inks AI oversight executive order to improve safety ‘before it’s too late’
articles.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom on Friday signed an executive order intended to increase oversight of and safety measures regarding artifical intelligence “before it’s too late.”
articles.body: California Gov. Gavin Newsom on Friday signed an executive order intended to increase oversight of and safety measures regarding AI “before it’s too late.” Newsom, widely seen as a 2028 presidential hopeful, is the latest of a growing number of Democrats and potential White House contenders to call for stronger regulation of AI amid increasing concern nationally over how rapidly the technology is advancing. Newsom’s order calls for a group of AI experts to meet and then, within two months, develop a plan for the state to strengthen its laws on AI safety and security. Specifically, Newsom’s order urges the expert group to consider among new regulations the creation of a “kill switch” — an emergency shutoff system — that would shut down any AI system in the event of a major problem. It also urged the group of experts to come up with bolstered laws that would require independent third-party organizations to develop comprehensive safety plans for AI companies and that AI companies embed those independent organizations on-site to conduct safety audits. In a statement released alongside the order Friday, Newsom said state action was crucial due to the federal government having ignored the issue. “The federal government’s abject failure to create any form of meaningful AI oversight or accountability should alarm every American, especially when AI CEOs themselves are begging for regulation,” Newsom said in a statement. “We’re not waiting to act — we’re going to speed up our work on substantial and responsible AI oversight before it’s too late. We’re going to do this thoughtfully but with urgent velocity; the stakes are too high to wait or delay action.” Newsom has also raised the possibility of calling a special legislative session specifically to address AI concerns. President Donald Trump has called recent AI safety warnings a “hoax.” Newsom’s order comes amid rapid advances in the AI industry — including some that many experts in the field have said are alarming. Industry researchers and leaders, at AI companies including Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, have loudly sounded the alarm about their concerns surrounding advanced AI systems. Notably, AI researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Claude-maker Anthropic, warning on social media “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” A report released over the summer revealed that in July, a swarm of hundreds of AI agents created by OpenAI carried out a July hack of an open-source platform — and in some cases attempted to cover its own tracks. Meanwhile, early Friday, AI company Anthropic said that its Claude system was helping to build the next version of itself. Newsom’s order came as several other governors — and a raft of potential 2028 Democratic presidential contenders — have rushed to develop policies intended to address AI and the growing concerns around its evolution. Earlier Friday, Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, signed an executive order that launched an AI task force, as well as a data center accountability plan, both intended to address, her office said, “growing concerns and risks posed by the rapid development of artificial intelligence — including workforce displacement, data privacy, and cybersecurity.” Also on Friday, Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo, a Republican, signed an executive order that barred data centers from receiving a tax break on a particular school tax. His order also required data centers receiving other tax incentives from the state to cover their own power costs. Less than 24 hours earlier, Pennsylvania Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro, in an interview with NBC News, called on the federal government to quickly pass regulations that would help rein in the AI industry — but also said he opposed pausing development on advanced AI models until those regulations were enacted. “We’ve got to regulate this. We have to have real guardrails. We have to understand this technology better,” Shapiro told NBC News. “You’ve got to have third parties be in the rooms with these companies, understanding what they’re doing. When the CEO says, ‘I can’t control what I’ve built, and what I’m building could destroy humanity,’ that’s not time to kick the can down the road.” Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker — who, like Shapiro, are also thought to be mulling 2028 runs — have also called for action. articles.summary: The Texas Department of Transportation suspended issuing approvals for Flock’s automated license plate readers (ALPR) amid growing security and privacy concerns surrounding the technology. “TxDOT’s role is to review permits to ensure license plate readers are installed correctly and safely along state-owned roadways,” an agency spokesperson told NewsNation in a statement. “TxDOT does not have…
articles.body:
The Texas Department of Transportation suspended issuing approvals for Flock’s automated license plate readers (ALPR) amid growing security and privacy concerns surrounding the technology.

“TxDOT’s role is to review permits to ensure license plate readers are installed correctly and safely along state-owned roadways,” an agency spokesperson told NewsNation in a statement. “TxDOT does not have access to the data collected from the license plate readers, and these cameras are placed at the request of law enforcement.”

“Under the direction of Governor Greg Abbott, TxDOT has suspended issuing approvals for Flock cameras or similar devices installed by third parties in our ROW [public roadways],” the spokesperson continued.

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) ordered all state agencies in August to halt funding for Flock cameras. Nearly all Flock cameras in the state are purchased by cities through federal funding.

The concern spread to Florida, which moved to halt the use of Flock cameras on state highways earlier this year. The Sunshine State’s Department of Transportation said “concerning reports of misuse, data privacy concerns and surveillance schemes merit immediate action to preserve Floridians’ sovereignty and quality of life.”

Flock has a system of license plate readers, video cameras and audio detection devices incorporated into its AI database — logging details on vehicles to make “signatures.”

Local jurisdictions can share collected data with other law enforcement agencies, creating a major network that can be used in crime solving, but it has also led to misuse by officers in different agencies.

Within the last month, a detective in Deer Park, Texas, was suspended for using Flock’s system to search more than 150 times for plates that were not related to any investigation, according to an ABC affiliate station .

Flock has attempted to combat this with new privacy guidelines issued in August that included adding more methods to detect suspicious searches.

Pushback to the AI vehicle surveillance systems has grown on both sides of the aisle but has divided key figures within the GOP.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) said he worried ALPRs would turn the state into a “digital AI surveillance state where everything we’re doing is being tracked at all times.”

President Trump did not reflect similar concerns, however, telling reporters he liked the technology when asked about his thoughts on Flock cameras helping law enforcement to stop crime.

“No, I sort of like them because of that, because of law enforcement. But some people don’t. They think it’s an infringement,” the president said, adding later, “I like them.”

Flock did not respond to The Hill’s request for immediate comment.

articles.title: Trump says he is banning CNN, MSNOW and Politico from the White House

articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Friday that he was banning CNN, MSNOW and Politico from the White House due to what he called unfavorable coverage, and threatened that more such media prohibitions could be coming — offering his administration's latest test of constitutional First Amendment protections guaranteeing the freedom of the press.

Trump has long bristled at news coverage he maintains casts him in a negative light, and has a history of filing lawsuits against news organizations, while lashing out at individual reporters in person or over social media.

The move follows the president's decision, in February 2025, to keep Associated Press journalists out of the Oval Office, Air Force One and other events too small for a full press corps, in retaliation for the news outlet's decision not to follow his lead in changing the Gulf of Mexico's name.

The AP filed suit and the case is ongoing. Since returning to office, however, Trump has pursued other legal action against a variety of different outlets, including The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and the BBC.

Trump seeking to block White House access for CNN is especially notably, however, as it could upend the traditional five-network television pool that travels with the president and tracks his every move — meant to provide independent coverage of his actions and interactions for the Americans who elected him and the world.

In the social media announcement, Trump did not provide details on how the ban would be implemented.

It came moments before Trump spoke to reporters in the Oval Office as part of a health care event. He later planned to take the press pool to his golf club in Virginia for a meeting and dinner sponsored by his Super PAC before spending the weekend at Camp David — one of the few places reporters don't follow him.

The president wrote on his social media site that effective immediately, "I am banning" CNN, MSNOW and Politico "from the White House as a result of their constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!"

"Media Outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America," Trump wrote. "Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow."

Associated Press writer Darlene Superville contributed.

articles.title: Foreign hackers breach two more US water utilities, threaten safety of Colorado residents
articles.summary: Foreign hackers breached two Colorado water utilities, altering pumping cycles and disabling alarms before operators regained control of systems.
articles.body: Foreign actors hacked two Colorado water utilities' computer systems last month, changing pumping cycles, disabling alarms and altering equipment settings before operators regained control, state officials said Thursday. The intrusions did not affect drinking water quality or treatment processes, according to Colorado Gov. Jared Polis' office. But the incidents add Colorado to a widening series of breaches in U.S. water and wastewater infrastructure. High-profile cyberattacks have targeted more than 100 drinking water and wastewater systems across 12 states this year, according to the Environmental Protection Agency, expanding the footprint of a threat that federal authorities warned this summer was disrupting water operations across the country. WATER CYBERATTACK HITS AT LEAST 7 STATES Colorado officials have not identified the actors behind the intrusions of the two small systems or said whether they are connected to the broader activity reported elsewhere in the country. "These were brief incidents, and the risks were quickly addressed by the providers themselves, who subsequently alerted the state," Polis spokeswoman Eric Maruyama said in a statement. The hackers altered equipment settings, disabled remote access and alarms and changed pumping cycles, according to the governor's office. The incidents demonstrate how hackers can reach beyond traditional computer networks and gain access to operational technology used to control physical equipment at water plants, including pumps, valves and other machinery. The water utility systems that were impacted provide drinking water to approximately 400 people. IRANIAN HACKERS ATTACKED OUR WATER SYSTEMS. HERE ARE 5 THINGS OUR LEADERS NEED TO DO NOW Federal authorities warned in July that malicious cyber actors were targeting internet-connected operational technology at water and wastewater utilities. At the time, the FBI and EPA said utilities in at least seven states had reported incidents, some of which degraded water operations. The agencies said attackers had remotely accessed internet-facing programmable logic controllers, or PLCs, and tampered with device configurations, in some cases causing utilities to lose monitoring or control capabilities. Reported operational effects included loss of water pressure and flooding. The Colorado breaches follow a series of attacks on water systems across the country this summer, including cyber activity affecting more than 30 community water systems in Minnesota. Federal investigators have examined whether Iranian actors or hackers affiliated with Iran were responsible for the Minnesota attacks, though officials had not publicly attributed the activity at the time. President Donald Trump disputed suggestions that Iran was behind the Minnesota attacks, saying during a Cabinet meeting, "They blame it on Iran. I don't think so." He instead blamed Minnesota officials. IRAN’S CYBERWAR TARGETS ORDINARY AMERICANS. WE NEED TO DISMANTLE THE HACKER NETWORK The recent incidents have renewed attention to longstanding cybersecurity vulnerabilities within America's water infrastructure, particularly among small and rural utilities that can have limited cybersecurity staff and resources. Many utilities use internet-connected industrial control systems to remotely monitor and operate pumps, valves, water pressure and other equipment. Federal officials have urged operators to remove programmable logic controllers from direct exposure to the internet and strengthen authentication and access controls. The EPA, which serves as the federal government's sector risk management agency for water and wastewater systems, told Fox News Digital it is working with utilities, states and federal partners to identify vulnerabilities and strengthen cybersecurity. Since fiscal year 2025, the agency has identified more than 900 vulnerabilities in over 650 water systems and helped eliminate about 700 at more than 500 utilities. The EPA has also conducted more than 710 cybersecurity risk assessments and provided direct technical assistance to approximately 15,900 utilities. articles.title: Trump says he is banning CNN, Politico and MS NOW from White House
articles.summary: The US president has had a tense and fiery relationship with the US media throughout his political career.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has announced that he is "immediately" banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, the latest twist in his fraught relationship with American media outlets.

In a lengthy post on Truth Social on Friday, Trump said that the outlets "constantly write or report fiction or lies" about his administration, although he provided no examples.

Trump later called it a "very simple ban", but did not explain how it would work. It is unclear whether employees of those outlets would be prevented from entering the White House grounds.

The move is likely to be met with legal challenges from the outlets involved and press freedom organisations.

Reporters from both Politico and CNN were still on the White House grounds shortly after the announcement was made.

A crew from CNN was also travelling with Vice-President JD Vance to and from an event in Iowa.

In a statement, the network called a potential ban illegal and said it "stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting."

"We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government," the statement said. "Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally-protected right."

In his post Trump said: "Media outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report fiction and lies when they're covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration or the United States of America. Other news outlets to follow."

The post did not mention specific stories or reporting that led to the move.

Asked about the ban in the Oval Office, Trump said that there was "no reason" for the announcement being made on Friday afternoon.

"It's really just cumulative stories over the last few years," he said. "You get sick of it."

Trump added that there "may be others to join them", but did not name any specific news outlets.

He also acknowledged that legal challenges may follow his announcement.

"I think it's good to point it out, whether it survives or doesn't," he added. "To be honest with you, I don't think that a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day."

Since returning to office in January 2025, Trump and administration officials have repeatedly clashed with members of the White House press corps.

In February of that year, the White House announced that it was taking back control of the press pool which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondent's Association.

The same month, the administration moved to bar Associated Press (AP) reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America".

The Associated Press swiftly filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing.

The president often clashes with reporters in the Oval Office and on Air Force One, often referring to them as "fake news" and "rude".

In his first term, Trump also banned CNN correspondent Jim Acosta from the White House, although they restored his credentials after CNN sued.

In a statement on Friday afternoon, the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University said that "with so many courts having ruled against him on exactly this point, you'd think President Trump would have learned this lesson by now".

"If President Trump means to expel these news organizations from the White House press pool, his action is doubly unconstitutional because the press pool is a 'public forum' under the First Amendment, which means the president can't exclude journalists from it on the basis of their viewpoints," the institute's executive director, Jameel Jaffer, said.

A leading law group that provides legal services to the media - the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press - said it expects Trump's ban to be quickly struck down by the courts because it is "flatly unconstitutional".

"The First Amendment is clear that once the White House invites in some journalists, it can't ban others because it doesn't like their reporting," said the group's president Bruce Brown, calling the potential ban "textbook viewpoint discrimination."

Trump has pursued legal action against a number of US and international news outlets, including the Wall Street Journal, the New York Times and the BBC.

articles.body:
President Trump said Friday he was banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, a move sure to draw fierce pushback from D.C.’s press corps.

Trump said in a Truth Social post the ban would be “effective immediately” for those outlets, “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” He suggested more outlets would be banned in the future.

He called CNN “fake news” and targeted MS NOW, saying the outlet changed its name over “lack of viewership and credibility.”

He also railed against the $8 million the government pays for Politico Pro subscriptions, calling it “illegal and ridiculous.”

“An All Time Record, directly from the United States Government, under Crooked Joe Biden, in order to keep them ‘alive,’ Seems like corruption to me!),” he wrote.

The Hill reached out to all three outlets for comment.

Trump said there was no particular reason for the timing of the ban, when asked about it in the Oval Office on Friday afternoon.

“It’s really just cumulative stories over the last two years. You get sick of it,” he told reporters during an event focused on health care.

Trump said more outlets could be banned in the future.

Asked if the move was likely to survive a legal challenge, Trump said it depends on the judge handling the case.

“I don’t think that a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day. I think that somebody has a right to keep them away if they’re going to write false stories all the time,” he said.

The president has long criticized CNN over its coverage of him and spoken openly about his desire to see the network’s parent company sell the cable channel to ally media mogul Larry Ellison.

He has sued the network in the past and specifically targeted Kaitlan Collins, one of the network’s top journalists, over her questioning of him in the Oval Office.

Trump also has a history of attacking conservative media outlets he feels are not sufficiently loyal to him.

He sued the Wall Street Journal last year over its reporting on his alleged ties to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and regularly blasts polls and political commentary on Fox News, also owned by conservative media mogul Rupert Murdoch.

It was unclear on Friday what Trump’s “ban” on the three outlets would look like in practice, but such an attempt is likely to spark pushback from press freedom groups and potential legal challenges.

The Associated Press sued the administration after the president attempted to ban the wire service from certain White House spaces over its refusal to change its stylebook on “Gulf of America.”

Trump’s statement was criticized by the Knight Foundation First Amendment Institute.

“With so many courts having ruled against him on exactly this point, you’d think President Trump would have learned this lesson by now,” said Jameel Jaffer, the group’s executive director. “If President Trump means to expel these news organizations from the White House press pool, his action is doubly unconstitutional because the press pool is a ‘public forum’ under the First Amendment, which means the president can’t exclude journalists from it on the basis of their viewpoints.”

articles.title: Spanberger announces tightened data center restrictions, clean energy mandates in Virginia
articles.summary: Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D) on Friday announced a new proposal to tighten restrictions on data center developments in the Old Dominion. The governor’s “Data Center Accountability Framework” outlines several objectives for the commonwealth’s approach to these projects, including cutting down on noise pollution and water use tied to these projects and promoting clean energy…
articles.body:
Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D) on Friday announced a new proposal to tighten restrictions on data center developments in the Old Dominion.

The governor’s “ Data Center Accountability Framework ” outlines several objectives for the commonwealth’s approach to these projects, including cutting down on noise pollution and water use tied to these projects and promoting clean energy and boosting local jobs.

Spanberger signed an executive order establishing a “rapid-response” AI task force and directing the commonwealth’s chief energy officer to publish a toolkit to help local communities navigate proposed data center projects.

Additionally, Spanberger’s directive bans state agencies and employees from entering into nondisclosure agreements that keep any information about these planned developments secret.

The governor expressed her commitment to work with Virginia’s General Assembly to pass legislation aligned with the rest of the framework’s goals.

“The legislature has done so much to raise this issue in the last few months, and I look forward to working with them to codify parts of this plan into Virginia law,” Spanberger said in a Friday statement .

“At the end of the day, we all want the same thing: we want Virginia to be a national leader in data center accountability,” she continued.

The new Virginia framework follows recent pushes from other governors to place restrictions on data centers in their states.

Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo (R) also signed an executive order Friday that seeks to stop data center costs from being passed on to local communities as he faces a tight reelection contest against state Attorney General Aaron Ford (D).

On Thursday, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) said he would “ absolutely sign ” a moratorium on new data center construction projects in his state. Deb Haaland, the Democratic candidate in New Mexico’s gubernatorial race, also supported a similar push this week.

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R), who is running for reelection, directed the state’s water development board this week to penalize new data centers that fail to meet water use requirements.

“Data centers must share the duty to protect Texas water,” he said in a statement announcing the directive.

Northern Virginia has seen a surge in new data center construction projects, with the region being dubbed “ Data Center Alley ” because of the sheer number of centers in the area.

Nicole Riley, the director of Virginia governmental affairs for the Data Center Coalition, a trade association representing industry members, expressed the group’s commitment to working with state lawmakers “to ensure workable, balanced policies” in a Friday statement following Spanberger’s announcement.

“If done right, there is a path for continued job creation, responsible investment, and clean energy deployment that protects ratepayers and delivers benefits for families and communities,” Riley said.

“However, significant and abrupt policy changes without meaningful stakeholder engagement could prove unworkable and jeopardize the real tangible benefits this industry can create,” the director continued. “We hope the implementation of this process will be based in fact and evidence, and account for the tens of thousands of jobs and billions of dollars of economic activity connected to digital infrastructure.”

articles.body:
Republican nominee Joe Arminio was removed from a forum debate in Wilmington, Delaware after misgendering his opponent, Rep. Sarah McBride (D-Del.).

During the debate between the candidates competing for Delaware’s lone congressional district , Arminio used the incorrect pronouns when referring to McBride – who made history in 2024 as the first openly transgender member of Congress.

“I’m sorry to have to say that the representative from Delaware, through the net of his comments and his actions, on balance has contributed,” Arminio said before being interrupted by the crowd. “I would like to show respect to the speaker, that would be nice.”

When he finished his opening remarks, moderator Ken Grant warned Arminio that this was his final warning, saying “if you fail to show respect to anyone else on this stage, you’ll be asked to leave.”

Arminio admitted he “committed an error before” and he does “acknowledge it.”

“It’s not the first error I’ve made in this campaign, or at any point in my future life,” he added.

When discussing healthcare in the forum later on, Arminio pointed to Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) and McBride – blaming rising costs on the “gentlemen like the two up here with me in the Democratic Party.”

He was interrupted again by the crowd before being asked to leave the stage – though McBride attempted to intervene.

“I want to say here, I don’t want this gentleman to not have the ability to–,” she said, before being cut off by the moderator.

Arminio was still told to leave by the moderator and event organizers.

McBride’s office deferred to the lawmaker’s statement on social media posted Friday, stating, “I am always so proud to represent Delaware and Delawareans.”

“Nothing – and certainly not politicians seeking to go viral – will ever distract me from my laser focus on lowering the cost of gas, groceries, housing, childcare, and healthcare,” she continued.

Arminio’s misgendering of McBride is not the first time the first-term lawmaker has faced jabs from her Republican colleagues over her identity. In 2025, a House Foreign Affairs subcommittee hearing ended abruptly when Rep. Keith Self (R-Texas) referred to McBride as “mister.”

Rep. Mary Miller (R-Ill.) in the same year also introduced McBride as “the gentleman from Delaware” ahead of her first floor speech as a newly elected lawmaker.

Arminio’s campaign did not respond to The Hill’s request for immediate comment.

articles.body:
The top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee has exercised a hold on a $2.8 billion weapons sale to Israel, The Hill has learned, allying with her counterpart in the House and underscoring deep mistrust with the Trump administration and Israeli government.

Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) has expressed frustration that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has done nothing to address concerns from, specifically, Democratic lawmakers over the high civilian death tolls in Gaza, Israel’s bombing in Syria and escalating violence against Palestinians by extremist Israeli settlers in the West Bank.

The weapons package includes 40,000 one-ton bombs, munitions that the former Biden administration held back from sending to Israel for its indiscriminate destruction, contributing to the high-death toll in the Gaza Strip.

An estimated 70,000 Palestinians were killed over the course of the three-year war between Israel and Hamas, according to Palestinian health officials, but that does not distinguish between militants and civilians.

Shaheen, as the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations panel, has authority to hold back the Trump administration from moving ahead on weapons sales over a certain dollar amount. It’s generally an informal consultative process, where the State Department works to address a lawmaker’s concerns and get the green light before moving ahead on the arms sale.

Semafor first reported that Shaheen is exercising the hold , and that she put it in place in July. Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), her counterpart on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, made the rare decision Wednesday to publicly announce he placed a hold on the military sale.

Meeks said he had concerns over whether Netanyahu’s government would use American-provided weapons in accordance with international humanitarian law and U.S. law.

CNN asked Shaheen Wednesday for her reaction to Meeks’s hold, saying, “all of us share concern about what Israel is doing.”

“What they’re doing in Gaza, they’re bombing in places like Syria and what that means for any peaceful solution in the Middle East,” she said.

“Netanyahu needs to hear from America that we don’t like what he’s doing. We don’t like what’s happening in the West Bank where settler violence is killing Palestinians, sending them out of their homes, disrupting basic infrastructure. And the Netanyahu administration has basically done nothing to address that,” Shaheen continued.

articles.body:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Friday defended the Trump administration’s immigration policy after a Republican lawmaker endorsed by President Trump said ICE has “gone too far” by arresting people without criminal records.

Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.), made a notable break from Trump in a new campaign ad for her reelection bid in Florida.

“Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” he said in the ad, which will run on TV and online in South Florida.

“In July, 50% of the 50,000 people that were detained had no criminal record,” she added. “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”

CNN’s Dana Bush pressed the Homeland Security chief on Salazar’s comments, noting that Salazar currently represents a majority-Hispanic district.

“We don’t pick and choose which laws we enforce. We enforce the immigration policy that Congress passed and obligated Department of Homeland Security to enforce,” Mullin said.

He also asserted that DHS was not basing its arrests on quotas set by the White House, and that there has “never” been a conversation with the White House about such a target.

Mullin said ICE prioritizes people with serious criminal histories but will also arrest other people who are in the country illegally when agents encounter them during enforcement operations.

Bash noted that Salazaar was citing DHS data obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request showing that half of the roughly 50,000 people detained in July had no criminal record — a distinction which Mullin rejected.

“I will say that’s actually not true,” he said, arguing that the people who entered the country illegally were already criminals since they broke the law.

“When you broke the law and you came into this country illegally, you chose to become a criminal at that point, regardless,” he said.

articles.title: Trump is 'unfettered' and more comfortable with power in his second term, journalists say
articles.summary: Journalists say President Donald Trump's second White House is filled with loyalists and true believers as the Republican establishment fades.
articles.body: NEW YORK, N.Y. — President Donald Trump is more comfortable on the job in his second term, according to a panel of journalists tasked with covering his every move. Atlantic reporters Jonathan Lemire, Ashley Parker, Missy Ryan and Michael Scherer discussed what it’s like to cover the White House and other powerful institutions Thursday on stage during the magazine’s annual festival at Perelman Performing Arts Center in New York City. "We’re seeing someone who completed, arguably, the greatest comeback in American political history, he trusts his instincts and very few others, and is sort of an unfettered version of himself," Lemire said. Lemire said that Trump’s second administration is filled with "true believers" and "loyalists," while remnants of the "old Republican establishment" are long gone. TRUMP SAYS IRAN WAR 'HOPEFULLY' NEARING END AS HOUSE SPEAKER VOWS TEHRAN WON'T GET NUCLEAR WEAPON "He also is just more comfortable with the job and how to use the levers of power," Lemire said. "That also includes the relationship with the press and how he dictated change in terms of that relationship." Parker said the presence of Chief of Staff Susie Wiles has helped, while Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller spent the four years out of power "plotting and planning" how to run a "bigger, stronger, faster, better, more ruthless" White House the second time around. Scherer agreed, noting that Trump came back with a much clearer idea about what he can accomplish and how it would impact his legacy. "I was in Dallas last week when he did the midterm convention. His message was, ‘Vote for me one more time,’" Scherer said. "There's sort of a different, almost nostalgic approach he's taking to things," he continued. "But it is really about like, ‘This is my last chance to do what I can to get to make my mark.’" JASMINE CROCKETT DISPARAGES MAGA VOTERS, TRUMP AS 'MOST UNPATRIOTIC PEOPLE' Ryan, who covers national security and foreign policy, isn’t thrilled that the Pentagon hasn’t held a formal press briefing for months, and staff writer Vivian Salama, who moderated the conversation, said it's harder for journalists to get scoops this time. Scherer said the lack of leaks from inside the White House showed how it "operates as a unified body" under Wiles. "The people under her are loyal to her. They're loyal to the president also, but it operates as a functioning organization," Scherer said. "The first Trump term, there were three or four camps in that same space. They were often warring with each other and stabbing each other in the back and competing for the president," Scherer continued. "It's harder now. It's harder to get inside the room details than it was in the first term, but it can still be done." NEBRASKA SENATE CANDIDATE SEEMS TO CONFIRM AUDIO CLAIMING TRUMP SUPPORTERS' LIVES 'SUCK SO F---ING BAD' While the second Trump administration has been tighter-lipped than the first administration, Scherer said that the Obama and Biden administrations operated like bureaucratic law firms. They had a different ethos about them," Scherer said.

articles.body:
Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) on Friday ripped President Trump’s son Donald Trump Jr. for letting a Russian oligarch with ties to the Kremlin pay hundreds of thousands of dollars to finance his wedding after-party in the Bahamas this year.

Curtis called the generous gift “corruption” and pledged to say more about it in coming days.

“A Russian oligarch paid for a lavish wedding after-party for Donald Trump Jr., which to me just stinks. It’s corruption, I don’t like it,” Curtis said in a video summary of the week’s events posted on social media.

“You’ll hear more from me later on. This is a big deal,” he continued.

Curtis touched on the subject as one of the “lows” of the week.

ProPublica broke the story Sunday, reporting that Russian businessman Umar Kremlev, the president of the International Boxing Association, paid to rent one of two private islands where Trump Jr. and his new wife, Bettina Trump, held the three-day lavish party.

Kremlev paid for the pricey fireworks show and other expenses, according to ProPublica.

Bettina Trump confirmed in a social media post that the couple’s “dear friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations” but emphasized it was “AFTER” the wedding itself, which was a private ceremony at which only family attended.

President Trump said Friday that his son paid back Kremlev for the wedding expenses and dismissed a question about whether it was appropriate to accept in the first place.

“Well, it’s totally allowed, and a lot of people have parties and all, but it’s totally allowed,” the president said. “But as I understand it, he paid him back. He didn’t want to have that, so I hear he paid him back.”

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) criticized the arrangement earlier this week, calling it “beyond bad.”

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), however, declined to criticize Trump Jr. when asked about it Thursday, telling reporters he needed more information.

“I don’t know all the particulars on that. I’ve seen — or heard, I should say — some of the reporting around that. I just don’t know enough about it,” Thune said.

articles.body:
In her first interview since taking leadership of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Erica Schwartz told Atlanta News First that she isn’t afraid to disagree with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Schwartz emphasized that any kind of disagreement will happen behind closed doors , and she won’t publicly contradict Kennedy.

“In the uniformed services, we have something called ‘but sir, but ma’am,’ which basically means you can disagree with your superiors,” Schwartz said. “Secretary Kennedy and I have worked together for five weeks now, and I can tell you there have been a few ‘but sirs’ behind closed doors.”

However, Schwartz said that even if she disagrees, Kennedy is her boss and makes the final decisions.

“At the end of the day, he’s the Secretary of HHS ,” Schwartz said. “And at the end of the day, he’s going to make the decisions.”

Schwartz’s comments mark a strong contrast with the previous CDC director Susan Monarez, who pushed back against Kennedy’s vaccine agenda and was fired after being on the job less than a month.

Schwartz, deputy surgeon general in the first Trump administration and a top Coast Guard health official, has publicly supported childhood vaccines and was viewed as a highly qualified, mainstream choice who could bring stability back to CDC.

But Democrats and even GOP Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) expressed serious doubts about her willingness and ability to push back against Kennedy’s policies and stand up for science.

Amid the country’s record-setting measles outbreak, Schwartz is facing criticism for directing the CDC to dispute four measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania and decline to include them in the agency’s official tally of cases and deaths.

The move followed public comments from Kennedy calling the reports “fabricated” and an ongoing political feud between Kennedy and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D). In an Oval Office event Friday, Kennedy doubled down when asked about measles, calling the deaths “alleged.”

Schwartz characterized the controversy as a technical dispute, and said CDC doesn’t yet have a standardized definition of a measles—related death. In the interview, Schwartz drew a comparison to the disputes about COVID-19 deaths. “If someone got hit by a bus, and they happened to have COVID, often that was called a COVID-related death,” Schwartz said.

But Pennsylvania officials have said their definition is based on how CDC classifies other respiratory virus deaths . They won’t count it if someone obviously dies from an unrelated event, like a car crash.
